REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to move:
That the interim and final reports respectively of the Hon. Mr. Justice Clarke, commissioner appointed to inquire into the alleged existence of corrupt or illegal practices in the election held in the electoral district of Athabaska, in the province of Alberta, on the 29th of October, 1925, which reports were laid on the table of the House on December 15, 1926, be referred to the select standing committee on privileges and elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend to explain what is the purpose of sending these reports to the privileges and elections committee?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Possibly, Mr. Speaker,
as this is a new parliament I had better give a few facts to the House regarding the petition, and at least one reason why these reports ought to be referred to that committee.
A petition was presented to this House in the early part of last session, on February 1st, I think, signed by A. C. Berry, of the electoral district of Athabaska, in the province of Alberta, alleging that illegal and corrupt practices had extensively prevailed in that election. The House received that petition, and a motion passed the House on March 18, 1926, for the appointment of a commissioner to conduct an investigation. On July 10th, the Hon. Mr. Justice Clarke, of Alberta, was appointed as commissioner, and he conducted the investigation, and made, as is stated in the motion, two reports to the government. In his interim report he stated that corrupt and illegal practices had extensively prevailed in that constituency. Further in that report he mentioned certain polls, a dozen or more I think, in which there was a tremendous amount of fraud committed such as stuffing
29S
Athabaska Election

ballot boxes, forging returns and other documents. He did not in his report make recommendations further than simply to present the findings of his investigation to the government and the House. It seems to me that one purpose at least-there may be others-is to examine the findings of Mr. Justice Clarke and to ascertain if it is not possible to provide ways and means whereby it will be impossible in the future to conduct elections in Canada in that manner.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before this motion is carried there are a few things that I would like to say regarding the motion to refer this petition to the committee on privileges and elections. While the commissioner 'held an extensive investigation and made a report, there are several things in connection with it which he did not deal with at all and which in fact he had no power to deal with. The report will show that a large number of individuals were guilty of corruption, illegal practices and such like. A certificate of indemnity was given to election officials covering the charge of forging ballots, putting their names on ballots which they were not so authorized to initial, and offences of that kind, but the commissioner did not deal and had no power to deal with a large number of other offences. For instance, the report will show that some of them were guilty of forgery, that is, that they had forged cheques which had been sent out to pay the expenses of election officials and had cashed those cheques and obtained the money. The report will also show that some of them were guilty of perjury; that they gave false evidence when called before the commission. Surely no one will argue that the commissioner had any authority to grant certificates of indemnity covering those cases, but the result is that those people have not been punished to date, and so far as I know no notice has been taken of the matter.

speechtext:
I did not quite catch
what the hon. member said. Do I understand that these parties to whom he refers are in the government service?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Some of them are and
I will deal with that in a minute if my hon. friend will let me pass it for the moment. It might be well to give a little review of the whole situation that was planned for this election. In the first place the returning officer's office was at a point called Lac la Biche about a hundred miles away from the centre of settlement. There is a twice-a-week train service in that part of the country; there is only one highway running north and south reaching the point and it is not readily acces-

sible. To the returning officer being allowed to operate at that point the electors took very serious objection. They objected to the Chief Electoral Officer, requesting that he move the returning officer. If the Chief Electoral Officer were not acquainted with that constituency, one might fairly assume that he did not himself know the situation; but he lived in the city of Edmonton for a good number of years, having been as a matter of fact a law partner in the firm of Short & Cross, the latter being one of the candidates in the election. Therefore, he must have had a considerable knowledge covering the whole situation.
The next point was that they selected as returning officer a man who admitted on the witness stand that he could neither read nor write. They did bring in two aides for him who could read and write. In fact they sent down to Seattle and they brought back two men, one named Lawler and the other Deyl to run this election. I am sure the name of Deyl will be quite familiar to some of those who have been in the Liberal party in western Canada for a number of years. I would be much surprised if the Minister of the Interior had not heard of Mr. Deyl in the old days.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Quite often.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext: When liquor licenses were granted in Alberta, he was the man who used to go around to the hotel keepers telling them that unless they made a contribution to the campaign funds, their licenses would not be renewed. He was a revenue producer. Mr. Lawler is also well known to some of my Liberal friends. I would be surprised if the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Blatch-ford) did not know him. I believe he rendered very effective assistance in the civic election in 1925. These two men came in and took control of the elections. To begin with the registrars refused to send out voters' lists and the committee that was in charge of that campaign in that election protested strenuously to the returning officer and to the Chief Electoral Officer. When polling day came we had in our possession something less than 100 lists out of a total of 235. That may seem a small matter, but when you come to examine the lists it will be very apparent that the plugging of those voters' lists was a part of the whole scheme of corruption. For instance, on the list covering the poll at Venice, there were 105 names, and the return from the poll showed that ninety-five people had come to vote, ninety-four of them voting for Mr. Cross and one ballot being rejected.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How did that happen?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They were experienced
men. They should not have had a rejected ballot. On an investigation of the names on the voters' lists it was found that there were probably thirty to thirty-five actually resident in the district. They were all on the list. Evidently the registrar started to put other names on the list, names of people who did not exist and who had not existed for quite a few years. As a matter of fact we found the name of one man who had been dead for twelve years and the return from the poll showed that a ballot had been polled under his name. Another man had been dead for three years. There were several men who had been out of the country for quite a number of years, including the priest of that district who was at the moment visiting in Italy. His name was, however, recorded in the voters' list as having gone to the poll and voted. It seemed also that in the compilation of the voters' lists they were endeavouring to break even between the males and the females, and when they put the priest's name on the list, to make the thing even they put the priest's wife's name on also. That is one registrar to whose being paid we objected, but a cheque was issued and went out covering the compilation of that list.
Another case which I would like to cite is that of three polls that were held in the forest reserve where nobody lives and where nobody is allowed to live. But those were not all the polls that were held there by any means. The evidence shows that three deputy returning . officers were instructed to take ballot boxes on election morning, follow up a trail that runs across this reserve, get back off the road about a half mile so that if anybody passed, they would not be seen, get into the bush and hold the election. All of this they did. Then they took the ballot boxes down to the Hudson's Bay store and proceeded to put in the ballots.
Now, is there any reason why this government should send out cheques for the compilation of those lists and to pay those deputy returning officers and poll clerks? Yet that is precisely w'hat has been done. We have heard of election irregularities in England, where there have been two or three outstanding cases, but there the electorate itself actually lost its head and either polled a corrupt vote or refused to allow some of the voters to exercise the franchise. This is a different case entirely. So far as this investigation shows, there is no evidence of any corruption on the part of the electorate; the corruption has been entirely on the part of the officials who were running the election. Inasmuch as those officials are the servants of this parliament, I think it i3 our duty to give due consideration to this case and to make certain that no future election in this country shall be conducted, in a similar way.
One other charge was mentioned a moment ago. A close scrutiny of those election officials will show that a large percentage of them are civil servants holding positions under the federal government. Take, for instance, one of the polls mentioned in this report, that at Lac la Biche. One of those who was found guilty of having put ballots in the box of people that never came to vote and was disfranchised-that is practically the only penalty the commissioner could enforce-is the postmaster of that village; he is also the sub land agent and in charge of the Dominion government telegraph service. I was notified this morning that he has resigned as postmaster. But it is four months since the report was made, it is two months since it was laid on the table, and all the time that man has been acting as postmaster and sub land agent and has been in control of the government telegraph service.
When those men who held the poll in the forest reserve were asked who told them to do so, they said it was a man by the name of Harry Bowtell. This Harry Bowtell is a rather interesting character-and also a civil servant. He is the postmaster at Frog Lake. He has held the office for seventeen years. I think he is also a sub land agent. I do know he is in charge of the Dominion government telegraph office. His wife is the assistant postmistress, and she admitted that when the cheques were being sent in -the name of people who did not exist she had knowledge that a couple of the cheques were coming to that office. As of course she knew no one would call for them, she signed the registration book for one cheque and got her thirteen-year-old daughter to sign for the other. Then they endorsed the cheques and cashed them. And yet Dominion government cheques have been sent to pay those people for such services in spite of the protests made by the people of Athaba'ska. We wrote -letter after letter to Ottawa trying to stop payment of those election officials, but a deaf ear was turned to our protests; those officials were paid.
I do not want to go into all these irregularities, there are so many of them, and I do not know that it is advisable to even attempt to do so. My purpose is to point out that these irregularities have been brought to the attention of the government, and that the government ha3 taken no effective way of dealing with them. The members of the
Athabaska Election

government practically shut their eyes to the whole thing. Section 87 of the Dominion Elections Act says that:
Any person who is, in any proceeding in which after notice of the charge he has had an opportunity of being heard, found guilty of any corrupt practice' or of any illegal practice, or of any offence which is a corrupt practice or illegal praetfce; shall, in addition to any other punishment for such offence by this or any other act prescribed be, for a corrupt practice during the seven years or for an illegal practice during the five years, next after the date of his being so reported, convicted, ordered, or found guilty, incapable of being elected to or of sitting in the House of Commons or of voting at any election of a member of that House or of holding any office in the nomination of the crown or of the Governor General in Canada.
I think that must have been inserted in order to give parliament special jurisdiction over these officials. True, under the criminal code, as under the Election Act, penalties are prescribed which can be enforced by a court, but this section applies particularly to the government and to parliament. In accordance with its terms these men were incompetent to hold any government position at the time that report was made, but we find they are still retained as government officials.
I charged a moment ago that the government has not taken any effective measures to wipe out this revolting situation. I think I can go a step further and very truthfully say that wherever that machine was weakened by reason . of this investigation those behind it have tried to make good the damage and in fact to strengthen their organization. In the village of Warspite the post office had been conducted in a store. The storekeeper sold out last fall. His successor was appointed postmaster by the postal inspector of that district. That man is reported to have been a very efficient postmaster. The post office guide shows that about eighty-five families get their mail at that post office. A petition signed by 150 people was sent to the Postmaster General's department that that m'an be left in charge of the post office, but a month or six weeks ago word came from Ottawa that the position must be taken away from him and given to another man. Every man and woman in the district signed that petition except seven. Evidently seven people in that district had influence enough to have the transfer made. I leave it to the House to say what is behind the transfer. Certainly tile transfer was not made because the new man was going to give better service. No one could argue that. If you are getting service that is satisfactory to 153 out of 160 people you are doing mighty well, and you are not safe in making any change.

Now, shortly before Christmas the French-Canadians of this country had a reunion at Ste. Anne de Beaupre. To that reunion came a Mr. Giroux, member of the legislative assembly -of Alberta. It is interesting to learn how he obtained the money to pay his expenses. The head office of the Dominion government telegraph service in Alberta is at Edmonton,, in charge of a man named Elmer. He sent out what is called a "twenty-three." It is a message sent over the lines to which all the operators are instructed to listen in. He told them about Mr. Giroux coming down here to interview the ministers and look after the superannuation of the operators, and that they would be requested, or commanded-I am not sure which-to put up five dollars apiece. He also wrote some telegraph operators down in Saskatchewan to put up a similar amount. I am told that altogether about $220 was secured for the trip. Now, is it in the interests of Canada that the civil service be used for obtaining political contributions? Let me go a step further. Is there a minister in the government who will get up this afternoon and say that Mr. Giroux interviewed him in any particular in the interests of the civil service? I do not think there is. He came down here to have a good time.
But the most regrettable point about this is that one man connected with the system who refused to make a contribution has since been reported to the department to his detriment. The hidden hand is trying to force him to contribute to Liberal campaign funds or else to blackmail him. I look across the House and I see quite a number of men who used to sit over on this side, who used to belong to the farmers' movement in western Canada. That movement was started largely-

speechtext:
Very well, Mr. Speaker,
I will deal with the report itself. I want to consider that portion of it dealing with the stamp of the returning officer. The situation in this regard was this: while the returning officer was at his office in Lac la Biche, the stamp was in possession of one Wilson in Edmonton, and the evidence would go to show that the ballots were taken over and given to Wilson, who stamped them. Now, the Elections Act provides that a returning officer shall keep the stamp in his possession, and as a matter of fact there is a severe penalty-I think it is five years-for anyone in illegal possession of it. Yet here you find a man in Edmonton who is in possession of the returning officer's stamp. I was amazed, indeed, to read the finding of the judge that he was legally in possession of it; I do not see for the life of me how he could be. However, the returning officer is now dead and I do not wish to bring him into the discussion, but I will say that during the time we had some criminal prosecutions out there he gave evidence, swearing that the ballots were sent to him at Lac la Biche.
At the very least, parliament should decide w'hen the stamp of a returning officer is legally in his possession and when it is not, and decide also whether or not the stamping of ballots in the city of Edmonton for a returning officer one hundred miles away is something that is in keeping with the instructions of the Elections Act. There was one other feature about the ballots which was lightly passed up in the investigation, and that is the fact that they were not all the same. On some there was a mistake in the spelling. My name was incorrectly spelled, as was also the name of Mr. Geauvreau, the Conservative candidate. Perhaps it is not remarkable that Mr. Cross' name was spelled correctly in both cases. The explanation of that irregularity in connection with the spelling of the names was that when they were printing the ballots, a sheet of paper got caught in the roll and some ballots were
spoiled. And that consumed a considerable quantity of paper that could not be accounted for. Then, the evidence goes on to show that a mistake in spelling the names was noticed and corrected, after fifteen or twenty thousand had been printed. This was called to their attention, according to the witness, by the returning officer over the long distance telephone. When you recall the fact that the returning officer could neither read nor write you wonder how in the name of common sense he could know. The printer's statement about the manner in which the paper was caught in the roll might account for the consumption of all the paper sent out by the Chief Electoral Officer, but it certainly does not account for the fact that there were two sets of ballots printed. Then, again, it was amply proved that ballots were sent by registered mail to several polls; and it was further established that two or three automobiles at least were driven from one poll to another by persons who were inquiring whether the officers had sufficient ballots, and assuring them that they could supply any deficiencies if need be.
Now, I consider all this a long way from being in accord with the instructions contained in the Elections Act, and I will conclude my remarks by requesting that this report be referred to the committee, that they be asked to submit definite findings covering the matter of the stamp, and that some recommendation be brought in to deal witli these officials. Certainly it is a disgrace to Canada if they are to be allowed to continue holding positions in the civil service while being guilty of such irregularities as have been proven in this report.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I did not,
expect when the motion was introduced that I should be drawn into the discussion, but in view of the utterly uncalled for remarks of the hon. member who has spoken (Mr. Kellner) I cannot allow the occasion to pass without some comment. Hon. members who were^ associated with us last year will recall that in our caucus, when the matter was discussed and this subject was brought to our attention, as to the corruption that prevailed in the Athabaska election, I was one who strongly insisted that we should stand behind the member for Athabaska, who had suffered from these malpractices, and that we should stand behind him even to the extent of affording him financial assistance in bringing the question before the House. In view of that fact, I feel that his remarks were absolutely uncalled for. We have had a number of references made to the position occupied by this group and I want to say that for myself, and

Athabaska Election
I believe I can speak for those more directly associated with me, I am not prepared to stand for anything in the way of electoral corruption. When the time comes, if it does come, we will be found insisting that those who have been directly responsible or in any way personally responsible for the practices which have prevailed, be visited with the l'uil penalty of the law. In view of this situation I think a very humble apology is due this group from the hon. member who has just spoken.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The attention of this House was
called to the famous Athabaska election for the first time during the course of last session, when a petition was presented to the House of Commons under chapter 8 of the revised statutes of Canada. The petition was signed by twenty-five or more electors of that constituency, and represented that the time for acting under the Controverted Elections Act having expired, a commission be appointed under the authority of this House, by the Governor General in Council, for the purpose of determining whether or not corrupt practices had taken place during that election. The House of Commons did act under that petition and requested the Governor General in Council to select a commissioner from various names contained in the motion, and a commissioner was appointed under the chapter I have already mentioned.
Under this law the commissioner must report to the Governor General the evidence taken and what he finds concerning the investigation, and that was done. Mr. Justice Clarke, who I am pleased to say is one of the most eminent members of the judiciary of Canada, made an interim and a final report, which mentioned certain persons as having been found guilty of corrupt practices. Section 31 of chapter 8 reads as follows:
Whenever it appears by the report of the commissioners under this act that any person named by them has been guilty of a corrupt practice and has not been furnished by them with a, certificate of indemnity, such report with the evidence taken by the commissioners shall be laid before the Attorney General of Canada, who shall, if in his opinion there is sufficient evidence available for a prosecution, certify such opinion to the Secretary of State, who shall thereupon communicate the report with the evidence to the Lieutenant Governor of the province in which the election was held.
When the interim report was forward by Mr. Justice Clarke the Solicitor General, who was then Acting Minister of Justice and Acting Attorney General of Canada, immediately sent it with his certificate to the Secretary of State, and when the final report was received

I myself did the same tiling. The requirements of the law were met, and if proceedings have not been instituted1, as to which I do not know, we would not be responsible; it is up to the Attorney General of the province of Alberta, who under the law must institute such proceedings.
_ Let me say to my hon. friend that as Minister of Justice I will be only to glad to associate a counsel with the local representatives of the province of Alberta in any proceedings which may be taken as a result of those frauds which took place during that election. I am in favour of the motion, and I may also say that if, as a result of this being referred to the committee on privileges and elections, some way may be found to prevent electoral corruption as it seems to 'have prevailed in that election, I and those who sit with, me on this side of the House will be only too glad to associate with my hon. friend in that respect.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the House
will agree with me that the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) has this afternoon made one of the most serious and most damning indictments against officers of this House and civil servants of this country that has been made in the parliament of Canada for many days. I noticed that when the motion was made this afternoon to refer these reports to the committee on privileges and elections, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) immediately asked, "For what purpose?" Until hon. members spoke in the House this afternoon the government would seem to have been lulled to rest with the idea that their full duty had 'been completed wben they delivered the reports to the Secretary of State and the Secretary of State in turn delivered them to the provincial attorney general.
The indictment laid before the House today goes much deeper than that. These reports of Mr. Justice Clarke have been in the hands of this government for four months, and the House will be anxious to know at this time what steps the government have taken under the law in regard to these election officials, and what steps have been taken in regard to the civil servants of this country who were guilty of gross wrong doing and in some cases of serious crime. I gather from the remarks of the hon. member for Athabaska this afternoon that many of these people are still in the service of the Dominion government notwithstanding the crimes that have been actually proved against them in that investigation. If this be so, what is the reason? Has the government taken no action in the matter? Has the government quietly taken

Athabaska Election
the position that having referred the matter to the local attorney general their duty is at an end? The Attorney General of Alberta has nothing to do with the civil service of Canada and he has nothing to do with our postmasters, so why has, not this government taken some action?
There is just one other thought in this connection. We had another investigation in the western part of Canada last year in regard to election irregularities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend leaves
that, is he laying down the principle now that every civil servant who took part in the election should be dismissed?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No; I am not, and my hon. friend should know that from my remarks. I am referring to those who are alleged to have been guilty of perjury, forgery and the like, as has been found by this report. Now I wish to refer to another case which came up for investigation last spring before the criminal courts of this country, in which the most gross frauds were proved. Officials of this House carrying on the elections were proved to be guilty of serious offences and were sentenced to severe penalties and terms of imprisonment. But I am informed to-day that two of these criminals have already been set at liberty although their full terms have not been served. I am also told that in the very near future another notorious official named Baldy Robb will also be given his liberty under ticket-of-leave, or by some process of the Department of Justice. I mention the matter in order, if I can, to stop the ticket-of-leave in that instance; I trust that the bringing up of this subject to-day will stop all negotiations for it. I was for a few days last July in the Department of Justice as acting minister. I know that Baldy Robb was sentenced about the beginning of May to a long term in the penitentiary, I think five years, and although he had only served from two to two and a half months at that time, already largely signed petitions, containing the names of political supporters of the government, were coming in from that western country asking for a remission of the penalty imposed. I hope Baldy Robb has not been granted any release or any ticket-of-leave. I hope none of those who were sentenced for irregularities last spring have been leniently dealt with. I hope also that this House will insist that this government take action at once in regard to those officials, those civil servants in the employ of this country, who have been found to be guilty of gross irregularities, and in many cases of serious crimes, in connection with the Athabaska election.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Edmonton, Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would not
have risen except for one reference of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner), namely, to my knowledge of Mr. Deyl and Mr. Lawler, although the hon. gentleman did not couple Mr. Lawler's name with that of Mr. Deyl. May I say that all who know the history of the province of Alberta are well acquainted with my actions in connection with all the chief actors who figured in this investigation?
Mr. Cross was attorney general in the government of which I had the honour to be the head. We disagreed, and he left the government, so that I take no responsibility for Mr. Cross.
With respect to Mr. Deyl, he was employed in the lands registry office at Edmonton, and left the service shortly after I became premier of the province. I never had anything to do with Mr. Lawler, nor was he ever employed in an official capacity while I had charge of affairs in Alberta. It seems to me that when this matter is referred to the committee the fullest investigation should be held. So far as I am personally concerned, I have no desire to shield anyone. My opinion is that everyone should pay the full penalty for his actions; and if anything can be discovered by the committee that will in any way prevent a recurrence of this sort of thing, I shall only be too happy to associate myself with such action and do all I can to forward it.
May I say, however, with reference to the remarks made by the leader of the opposition, that while I followed the newspaper reports -because I may say for the information of the House those reports were coming out every day during our election campaign in Edmonton last fall, and they were not doing the Liberal party any particular good, especially my colleague and I in the city of Edmonton-I had no knowledge that there was any official of the Department of the Interior implicated in any of these irregularities. Perhaps I have been recreant in my duty inasmuch as I have not read Judge Clarke's report in its entirety, but if amongst those mentioned in that report there is any employee of the Department of the Interior, employed even in the most humble capacity, then he or she will be dismissed at once. A question has been brought before the House by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), and I have no doubt that every member of this House, no matter to which party he may belong, is of the one opinion, and that is that every man who has been implicated in electoral frauds should be prosecuted without mercy, and that justice should prevail.
When Mr. Justice Clarke was appointed by the government, an investigation full and complete was held. Reports were made, two in number, the first being an interim report, and the second a final report. When the interim report was transmitted to Ottawa, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) being away at the time attending the Imperial conference, and I being then acting minister, I followed the law to the very strictest letter and in the very strictest spirit, and saw that every means was taken in order that the reports should be dealt with according to our law, and I do not think that any fair criticism can be made of the attitude and conduct of the Department of Justice in relation to the reports filed by Mr. Justice Clarke. Proceedings, if any are to be instituted, are to be instituted not by the federal' authorities, but by the provincial authorities of the province of Alberta, and the attorney general of that province is at perfect liberty to institute whichever proceedings he may deem mete. The law provides that in so far as the Attorney General of Canada is concerned, he may appoint counsel to act in conjunction with the counsel appointed by the provincial government. My learned friend the Minister of Justice stated a moment ago that this government was perfectly willing to do so if occasion should arise.
In conclusion, when these two reports are laid before the committee on privileges and elections, I believe that every member sitting on that committee will be moved by one, common spirit, and that is to try and de-32649-20
vise means of preventing any such things happening in the future as were proved to have happened in that constituency in the election of 1925.
As Solicitor General, having in charge the remission branch of the Justice department, I wish to make answer to the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) in regard to the paroling of two persons convicted of electoral frauds in the constituency of Peace River. The leader of the opposition mentioned the case of Baldy Robb. Firstly, Baldy Robb is in no way connected with the Athabaska election, and has absolutely nothing to do with Mr. Justice Clarke's reports. His activities were confined, and we may thank heaven that they were, to one constituency-the constituency of Peace River. I realize, listening to what has been said in this House this afternoon, and listening to the question put by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell), how careful we must be when dealing with remission cases. Reproaches have been levelled at me for having taken certain action. My hands, Mr. Speaker, are tied, and the leader of the opposition knows it. He has been Solicitor General in former governments, and he knows that every record in the remission branch, for motives and reasons of public interest, is confidential and cannot be brought before this House. I shall treat these files as confidential. I shall not try and screen my own responsibility by bringing before this House facts which are supposed, in the public interest, to remain confidential. The decisions which were taken were decisions which I took after mature consideration of all the circumstances. I have been a member of the bar of my province for over fifteen years. My family possesses certain judicial traditions which I cannot ignore, and my reputation as a member of the bar puts me away beyond any imputation that I might have been actuated by political motives.

generally, the investigation of what can be done to insure the public will being expressed without being subject to temptations, on the one hand to the coercive power of government, and on the other to the destructive power of corruption. These things are not matters that should be lightly treated. During the time that I have lived in western Canada-and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has made some reference to his experiences there- in certain parts of the west for a period of twenty-five years a studied system of corruption prevailed. An effort was made on a large scale to prevent the public will finding expression. I do not think we should blame parties in that respect at all. I know what the temptations are with respect to matters of that character. We know that decent, respectable citizens will not lend themselves to those things; but we know there are camp followers, men behind, men who are not only coiTupted themselves but who are willing to corrupt others. We know there are men who are ready and willing at all times to do What we are pleased to call "dirty work", and then after the matter is over they come and ask administrations and sometimes they brow-beat administrations to give them consideration to which they are not entitled.
The Minister of the Interior referred to two such persons this afternoon and I quite agree with him that they occupied in Alberta positions which they should not have occupied. They did work which has had a baneful and injurious effect upon the public life of that province. The same thing happened in Saskatchewan. We had in the journal of that legislature, as read here last session, a record of that condition of affairs. This House should use its every effort to stop that sort of thing because, if we do not prevent, it, our very democratic institutions are destroyed and responsible government has indeed become valueless in this country. That is the reason that the motion made this afternoon by the hon. member meets with my approval, although not with the hope that we shall be able at once to change this condition of affairs.
A very distinguished statesman, the late Dr. Weldon, came into this House of Commons, and he was so impressed with the dangers to democracy on account of the conditions to which I alluded, that he endeavoured to place upon the statute books short provisions whereby men might lose their franchise under certain conditions. This has been a dead letter although he had hoped for great things of it, and one of the real difficulties that threatens the life of this country to-day is electoral corruption on a very large 32649-201
scale throughout this Dominion. When I say "electoral corruption" I do not mean going out and buying votes. That is not what I have in mind at all. I mean the means used by which the free will of the people cannot be expressed, by which enormous sums of money are expended in an ordinary election, and it seems to me that we should follow the method which they have been compelled to adopt in England of limiting the amount of money that may be expended in elections.
I remember a friend of mine travelling on the train not long ago after the election of 1925, saying that two passengers on the train had been speaking and one said to the other that Bennett had spent $70,000 in the election in West Calgary. I am pleased to say that the return which I made covered every single sou that was expended by me with respect to that election and the election of last fall. But elections cost too much money and moreover so do the contributions that are enforced for the purpose of enabling them to be contested. We should have recourse to the provisions that obtain in the English law, whereby a limit is placed upon the amount that may be expended in any one constituency. In England, as hon. members know, the member has to pay the sheriff or the returning officer with respect to these things. I look upon the reference of this matter to this committee as affording an opportunity for it to make recommendations in regard to amending the statutes to which I have referred.
It is also not right to say that the blame attaches to any one party. I do not believe that, because I know there is no magic in belonging to one party in so far as virtue in an election is concerned. The whole fact is that sometimes those who are opposite to us are more astute in being able to manipulate the public will than we are, with a result that is detrimental to this country, returning them to power and leaving us in the opposition. That is another matter entirely; but astuteness in manipulation comes only from long practice, and it will be remembered that the Liberal party was in power for a much longer time in Canada, from 1896 to 1911, than the Conservative party was from 1911 to 1917. I suppose in the minds of some hon. gentlemen that may account for the result. It seems to me, however, that men should not occupy public positions and receive public moneys in this country who have been convicted of offences to which I have alluded or who have made confessions to that effect.

I was about to say that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) had confused two matters, and I know enough about government, without being instructed by the Solicitor General, to be aware that in matters affecting the release of prisoners it has been customary from time immemorial for ministers to speak to the law officers of the crown. I remember distinctly the case of Baldy Robb and two others being spoken to during the fall. I recall an expression of my own opinion with respect to the matter to the effect that it was important that an example be made. It is far more important 

this is the attitude I took-that the law should be vindicated, though not vindictively, and that its majesty be upheld than that feelings of sympathy should prevail in relation to any individual. We have all experienced those things; every man in public life knows that he has to make the choice between sympathy and public duty. His sympathies naturally impel him to do what the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) rose in his place to-day and so admirably stated- " I signed a petition for the parole of these two prisoners, for the reason that my sympathy found expression in the act." That was done to change and mould the opinion of the Solicitor General and of the Minister of Justice favourably towards the request. But as a public servant, owing a duty to the public, it is not open to any public man occupying a position of trust to sign any petition for the release of any prisoner under a system of ticket-of-leave. And we all know it. Time and time again I have had to refuse such requests by virtue of my representative position. I could not act in my capacity as a private citizen and lend the support of my official authority to a petition of that character, however it might affect the friendly disposition of the Minister of Justice or of the Solicitor General, whose human sympathies we all take for granted and whose desire to do what the Solicitor General describes as justice we do not question. But there is no such thing as justice with respect to tickets-of-leave; it is merely
a question of the exercise of discretion, founded upon judicial opinion, sometimes that of a judge, sometimes the views of penitentiary authorities or, perhaps, those of persons in charge of gaols, as to whether or not the release of a particular individual will enable him to start over again, to begin a new life under fresh conditions and overcome the peculiar difficulties that surrounded him in his first o.r second offence, as the case may be. Everyone who has read the life of that leader of the church army in England, Prebendary Carlisle, will understand thoroughly what has been done with reference to matters of this sort. Now and then it is possible to pick out a man and ito say, " Here is material out of which a real man can be developed. Here is a case in which a ticket-of-leave may safely be granted." Where there has been inexperience in connection with the commission of a crime, or where the other factors are such as to render it advisable, one may support the granting of parole. But in the case of a man of a notorious past, who has exercised political influence improperly in days gone by for one party or the other, it is important that the law should be vindicated in order thait the public at large may appreciate the inevitable character of the consequences that follow' upon wrongdoing. People should be made to understand that forgery, the manipulation of ballots, the destruction of ballot boxes, the marking of ballots otherwise than in the manner contemplated by statute are all contrary to the law and that any violation of the law in any of these respects shall be visited with rigid puishment, so that those newcomers who are to attain Canadian citizenship shall respect the institutions of the country. They should be made to understand that such lawbreaking as this is not to be tolerated, and that the law will be enforced whatever may be the result.
That is the attitude we should take with respect to such a question as this, and that is the reason attention is directed to it this afternoon. No one has any vindictive feeling against Baldy Robb. I have known him for over fifteen years and, were I to consider feelings of sympathy alone, I should desire to do him a good turn to-morrow, just as I would any other man, whether he were for or against me. But I cannot permit myself to become a party to the release of one who has boastingly said, "I have the power and the influence to be out of gaol almost before I get there." And this was his boast made
Athabaska Election

openly as reported in the journals of the country at the time. For these reasons I support the motion of the hon. member for Athabaska, in the hope that the members of the committee, realizing the enormity of these offences-although sometimes some of us may be tempted to smile at what we may consider something not so grave-which threaten the life of our democracy, which are injurious to the very wellbeing of our responsible institutions, and which in the long run will sound the death-knell of the things about which we should be greatly concerned. It is, I say, for these reasons and in the hope that the committee will make, with respect to the Elections Act and the Civil Service Act, as well as other statutes, such suggestions as will ensure the ordered and well regulated conduct of elections, free from the conditions that have obtained in Athabaska and Peace River, and in the hope, further, that we may be able to place upon the statute books a greater safeguard in the light of these occurrences, that I propose to give my support to the motion which has been introduced.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORTS OF MR. JUSTICE CLARKE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
With regard to appeals to the Department of Justice for remissions or tickets-of-leave, this is a matter that must depend upon the judgment of individual members of the House. I have myself on one occasion sent a letter to the department stating that I was prepared after a thorough investigation to stand on the floor of the House and support such a remission, and I would do the same thing again if a similar occasion arose, because the fact that I am a member of parliament does not deprive me of my right as an individual member of society to see that justice is done. The case to which I refer had nothing to do with election trials or frauds; it had to do with a temporarily insane man who was found guilty of having $2.50 or less in his pocket, which money, during the period of his insanity, he had not returned to his principals, and who was sentenced to the penitentiary for a term of three years. I considered this an injustice and said so, declaring that I was prepared to vindicate that stand in the House of Commons.
I trust, however, Mr. Speaker, that when this report is sent to the committee on privileges and elections they will feel that they have the sanction of the House for making a pretty thorough inquiry into the whole matter of the preparation of the electoral lists. I do not know anything about the preparation 
of such lists in other provinces, but I have had experience for two years in one constituency in the island of Montreal. I am blaming no one; I make no charges, but I shall say what I found there.
In the election of 1925 I was convinced, from the reports of my committee, that there were a large number of names on that list of persons who had no residence within that constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George, and who had not resided there for many years. After the election was over, in order to satisfy my curiosity, I employed a number of men who were experts in the preparation of directories and publications of that character, and I had them working during the months of November, December, January, February and March. Throughout those five months they went through the constituency finding out what names were on the lists for the election of
1925	of persons who were not residents in the constituency, and they found that over 2,000 fictitious names were on the federal list, some 900 impersonations having been voted in the election by means of this false list, not one of them voting for myself.
When it came to the preparation of the electoral list for the last election of 1926 I had a store of information available. My committee had to send out men ito ascertain whether on a certain date in May persons of the same names were entitled to be on the list. We received a return from the provincial reviser for the city of Montreal, and tracing down that provincial list which we received in
1926	as a basis for the preparation of the list for the federal election of 1926, we found over
2.000	fictitious names on the list for the federal constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George, these names having been derived from the provincial lists. We did nothing behind anyone's back. We made a list of these fictitious names and gave the committee of our opponents complete access to it. We also gave them a list of over 2,000 individual affidavits which we had prepared in order to make a proper legal protest (against these names being retained on the federal list for that district. Now, the preparation of 2,000 individual affidavits after
2.000	individual searches is an expensive matter. The committee on the other side, talking a list of over 2,000 found 175 or thereabouts which they said were the names of persons resident in the district formerly, who had removed to some other street in the district. They acted as fairly in the matter as we did, and I give them every credit. They desired to see that the revision was properly done, after their attention had been directed to the

Supplementary Estimates
matter. We each sent one representative to run down these 175 names in dispute, but I do not know what came of it, because I personally paid no more attention to the matter.
I do say that there is something radically wrong in the preparation of the lists in such a constituency as St. Lawrence-St. George when '2,000 fictitious names may be incorporated in the federal lists from the returns of the provincial revising officer. When the local provincial revisions was recently going on, I thought, although I may never run another election in St. Lawrence-St. George, that out of curiosity I would find out how the provincial list in the city of Montreal was prepared, and, during the last revision a couple of months ago, I sought to check the names going on the provincial1 list for the two provincial constituencies of St. Lawrence and St. George. I found that under our system of provincial registration in the city of Montreal, it is possible for a person residing in or purporting to reside in St. Lawrence or in St. George to register his name for those districts with any registrar in any other electoral district of the island of Montreal, so that in order to check the names going on the lists for St. Lawrence and for St. George I would have to send fifty of sixty representatives to fifty or sixty registration booths in all parts of the island, covering constituency after constituency -an impossible task, and one far beyond my financial resources.
But I will defy any man in the city uf Montreal or elsewhere to point to one single dollar spent by me or by my committee in those two last federal elections for any improper purpose. There was not a single dollar expended which was not vouched for. If I remember correctly, in order to secure a proper revision of these lists, and to see that no fraud was perpetrated, the expenditure in the 1925 election ran up to something like $25,000 while in the election of 1926 it was something like $14,000. I am trusting to memory. Now, there is $40,000 which a candidate for the House of Commons from that constituency is compelled to spend, not one dollar of it being devoted to fraudulent or corrupt purposes, but simply for the purpose of securing as correct a list as possible, and for the further purpose of preventing the impersonation of voters at the election. Talk about limiting the expenditure of money, as the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Bennett) suggested! Before you limit the expenditure of money in an election under conditions such as these, you must take efficient means to secure a reliable registration list.
As I am saying this I am glad to note that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) nods his assent, because I will say that he and many of his friends on the Liberal side in the city of Montreal take exactly the same position as I take, and leading Liberals of Montreal are as anxious as I am, I believe, to have a correct list. I am making no partisan charge in that regard, but as I will soon disappear from the political stage, I wish that there may be in Montreal an opportunity for the younger men who are making their way in the industrial, commercial and professional life of that city to play their proper part as candidates for elections to this House. There are manv such young men who would be worthy representatives of that city, but owing to the expenses, which are so great, they are utterly deprived of the possibility of ever being elected, no matter what may be their personal efficiency or qualifications for the position. Therefore I do trust that, on both sides of the House, out of the experience of the past and out of the experience of those intimately connected with these elections, we may find some way of procuring an efficient revision, so that when the results are known we may be confident that they are the results of an honest vote on both sides.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. PI. C. HOCKEN (Toronto West Centre): I ask the Minister of Immigration and Colonization if it is the intention of his

Special War Revenue Act
department, or of the government, to discontinue the financial assistance which has been given heretofore to the immigration work of the Salvation Army.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speechtext: I may say there is no intention of discontinuing the grant for assistance that the Salvation Army get in bringing out immigrants. As I said yesterday in reply to questions that have been asked me, they are getting exactly the same treatment that other people engaged in that work are getting. The army is receiving a grant this year of $25,000 cash for the work that they have been doing. Now, the Dominion government with the Imperial government are paying the passage of the boy immigrants that the Salvation Army are bringing out, and that money is being devoted to that purpose. If the army undertake settlement work along the lines that the Vimy Ridge organization, for example, are carrying on in the province of Ontario, they will receive exactly the same treatment. They will receive no direct grant next year other than the assisted passage paid jointly by the Imperial and Dominion governments.
I simply want to get a clear idea of the situation. I understand from the minister that no assistance is to be given to the army in bringing out boys. Is that the idea?
They are getting the assistance of the passage which is paid, the same as other organizations.
Is that an imperial arrangement?

No, it is an Imperial and Dominion arrangement under which the Dominion will pay a sum in hard cash on every boy that comes out, and which will amount to quite a large sum in the aggregate. I may say for the information of my hon. friend that some little trouble has arisen over the aftercare of boy immigrants. The Salvation Army have claimed or sought a grant because they give after-care to these boys. The department, however, have taken the stand that they have a fully equipped staff capable of giving the after-care to boy immigrants, and consequently that they 'are not justified in making a grant to the army for doing exactly the same work that they are doing. We shall
always be glad to have the Salvation Army, or any other organization, give whatever care they deem necessary to the immigrants they are particularly interested
