maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Edmonton, Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 55, to provide for special control by the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs of certain islands in the St. Lawrence river being part of the St. Regis Indian reservation.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

St. Regis Indian Reserve
On section 1-Short title.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I think the
minister had better explain what this bill is intended to do.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: The explanation is really all contained in the preamble of the bill. For a great number of years there have been long leases, ninety-nine year leases, granted on certain islands in the St. Lawrence river owned by the St. Regis band of Indians. No Indians have been residing on these islands, and the islands have been leased for this long period at very nominal sums. It will be noted from the preamble that the department has taken action in some cases. Some of the leases have matured, and in other cases action has been taken to break the leases, and the islands are designated in which that has been effected. Further court action is pending in regard to the other islands.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Did the courts
annul these so-called leases in all cases?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Yes, except
in those cases that are still pending. We have succeeded in recovering Lewis island, Snyder island, and Thompson or Macmaster island, and actions are still pending in respedt of Thomas or Hamilton island, and what is known as the Easterbrook farm on Cornwall island. It is considered that the revenues derived from these leases are not neatly adequate for the land that is under rental, and we propose to lease them at rentals that will be more commensurate with their value, the proceeds going to the maintenance of the band of St. Regis Indians.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Is anybody complaining that this is causing them an injustice?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
We have
felt that it was an injustice to the St. Regis band that these islands should be leased at such low rentals, and we desire to secure rentals that will be more commensurate with the value of the property. This property of course has become much more valuable in recent years for summer resort purposes and will bring a much higher rental. There was in the old lease a provision that there could be a renewal at the termination of the first lease, so this is what we are doing.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Are the present
lessees of these islands under the Indian title complaining of this action of the government?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Not that
I have heard. The only request I have had registered is that those already in possession under leases should be given the first opportunity to re-lease.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I suppose the
minister will agree to that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Yes, I
think they are entitled to that.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
How long is it since
these leases were first issued?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I have not
that in my notes. The leases were for ninety-nine years with a provision in the lease for renewal at the end of that period.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Do these leases purport to be given by the Indian band?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Yes. They were at all events given by the consent of the band.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Were these leases in
writing?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Will any of
these islands likely be affected by the St. Lawrence power development?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I cannot
give that information.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Were the leases signed by
the Indians or by the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: By both, I am given to understand.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Superintendent to have power to deal with certain islands.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
It seems to be
all right that the department is only to deal with these lands when the old Indian leases are declared by the court null and void. I notice that clause 2 reads that the department may-

grant leases, licenses or other concessions without tlic necessity of obtaining a surrender of the said islands from the band.
I do not see anything in this bill stating that the proceeds shall go to the St. Regis Indians, although I understand that is what will happen.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
The Indian Act provides in all cases for that. When we come to discuss the amendments to the Indian Act my hon. friend will note that all proceeds of leases go for the benefit of the
St. Regis Indian Reserve

band. But as we are not selling the property, but simply taking power to lease these islands, we have inserted in clause 2, this provision to which my hon. friend has referred. These lands are being leased in the interest of the band themselves.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Is it not customary to obtain the consent of the band with respect to any dealing with their land?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Yes. In
cases where the band is in residence upon the reserve, the Indian Act provides for the consent of the band being obtained, and it is obtained in the ordinary way through their council. But in cases such as this where the Indians are not residing on the land, but it is part of the reserve and the reserve is being used for other purposes, we are asking for power to deal with these lands in this way.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Is the minister sure that
these islands are not at or near the proposed development in the river St. Lawrence? They are near Cornwall.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I cannot
say.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Would they be used for
purposes of the development?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: If they are, of course action would have to be taken to get possession of them.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I do not think there
should be any alienation of them.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Compensation undoubtedly would have to be made to the Indians for the land.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
But there should be no
alienation of the islands jin the meantime.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: We are not asking that power. We are asking power simply to lease them. There will be no alienation of the land from the band itself.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
These islands
should be held as far as possible under public * control until it is decided whether in any case they will be required for that development. No leases should be granted in the meantime where such interests might have to be expropriated.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
In this
legislation we are endeavouring to get away from long leases. Values change very rapidly. Five years are the limit in leasing this land, and in most cases the leases run from year to

year. I have not had any representations made to me with respect to leases; but if this should come under the St. Lawrence development, undoubtedly either a sale would be arranged, or the authorities who are dealing with the matter would expropriate the land under the Expropriation Act.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: I thought the leases were for the purpose of summer cottages and the like. It strikes me that one of the engineers in my hon. friend's department told' me at one time that some of these inslands would be utilized for dam or bridge construction work if the development went on. I think it would be well to safeguard that possibility, because in the event of a five or ten year lease, we might have to expropriate not only the lease but some buildings and the like. There should be a saving clause of some kind.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Something
of that sort will occur on these islands. It is occurring on all the islands, and these are not an exception.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I have been
reading over this proposed legislation, and really it seems to me the only power it gives to the government Which it does not have now is to lease these islands without the consent of the band. There is a long preamble telling about the old leases, how they have been cancelled by the court, and how the department is not going to deal with any of these islands unless the old title has been extinguished by the court. Then the bill simply goes on to say, in clause 2, that the department may lease the islands without the consent of the band. I see nothing else in the bill. :

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
That is
quite true. This property has never been occupied by the Indians. It is being maintained for their benefit. In cases where we execute leases for grazing or agricultural pur. poses on the reservation itself, where the Indians are in occupation, the act provides that the Indians shall be consulted. But this is just where the difficulty arises in this case. These lands are not occupied by the Indians and these long term leases have in the past entailed considerable difficulty. In some cases we want to get absolute control of this property for the benefit of the Indians. That is the reason we are asking for this bill.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Is there any precedent for the department dealing with the lands of an Indian reserve without the consent of the Indians?

St. Regis Indian Reserve

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
We have
that in the Indian Act. Under the recent amendment to the Indian Act we may take that action, but it 'has not been taken, with the exception of this case. That is why I suggested a bill for the purpose.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Why does the
minister need a separate bill?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
In some
particular cases it becomes necessary that we have the authority; but as I say it has never been exercised, because we have always been able to deal amicably with the band, and I am against it in any case where the band is in residence. This is a different situation altogether. A great deal of controversy will arise in connection with leasing these islands and the Indians who do not reside upon them are constantly 'having representations made to them. We are asking for fairly drastic amendments to the Indian Act, not applying to lands upon which the Indians reside. We are asking in the next bill for some supervision over individuals who seek to act legally for Indians, to solicit subscriptions from them, and so forth. This bill is primarily for the purpose of giving us control of these islands without reference to the band itself.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Is there no general clause in the Indian Aot to the same effect?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Not giving
the power that is asked for here.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
There is a band of Indians
in whom the ownership is nominally vested now?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Yes, the Regis band. They will get any profits that accrue from the administration of the land.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Why should not the Indians be consulted if it is Indian property?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: For the simple reason that this is a group of little islands on some of which there is timber and most of which are of great natural beauty, and we find the utmost difficulty in getting the Indians to agree as to who should have them. We are also troubled1 by people going to' the Indians and agitating them about leases. If we can have control of these islands we shall be able to get a very considerable revenue, which will assist very materially in looking after the welfare of this band.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
If the Indian department
does not try to get more revenue than it has in other cases of Indian land that it has let without the consent of the band, its control will be to the detriment of the Indians. For
my part I do not like to see this House pass legislation removing the land altogether from * any right the Indians may have as to its disposition. I brought a case to the attention of this House two years ago where the Indian department deliberately leased land against the vote of the Indians at much less than could have been obtained for it had it been leased by auction or on any other competitive basis.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is a fixed rate at which Indian lands are leased by the department, six cents per acre for pasture land for cattle and ten cents per acre for sheep. The lease mentioned by my hon. friend carries that rate. For some considerable time we had a great deal of agitation in connection with that case, but I have heard nothing of it recently. Just as valuable land as that referred to is leased for identically the same figure. As one who has to take responsibility for the administration of the Indian Act, I may tell the House that in certain cases we need this authority. We have a great deal of trouble in the administration of the Indian Act. There are agitators in every band, and there are also outside agitators who excite the Indians and give them a false conception of their rights. That has happened on more than one occasion since I have been in charge of the department. I am merely asking here for what is obviously necessary in order to protect these islands and to secure from them a revenue commensurate with their worth for the benefit of the band.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
What is the
area of these islands?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I cannot
give my hon. friend that information.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in connection
with the reserve which I mentioned a moment ago, I would ask the minister if the Indian department did not there do exactly what he iis asking authority for under this bill with respect to these islands? The department simply went ahead and leased that Indian land without the consent of the band, although the band had voted against such leasing. If the department had power to do so in that case under the general act, I do not see why the minister need come now and ask for this special act to do what seems to be the very same thing in connection with other Indian lands.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the lease in question was fully discussed here and I gave an explanation of every detail of it. Due consideration was given to
St. Regis Indian Reserve

the whole matter by the commissioner in * western Canada, and on his recommendation we made the lease. In certain instances we have power to override agitators in any band We have difficulty at the moment on the Six Nations reserve, and I say frankly that I think the trouble has come about largely because I have tried to be lenient with those Indians. I find in some cases that is not the best policy to pursue, for there is not a single band in which there is not a fair percentage of agitators, who thrive on agitation in preference to working for their living Those agitators can always stir up a great deal of difficulty for the department. There is a very valuable revenue to be secured from these islands.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: I am at a disadvantage because I have not the Indian Act before me, but is there not a provision in that act empowering the superintendent general to go ahead without the consent of the band and lease unoccupied lands as he sees fit?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Not to give us the authority we want under this bill.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
It seems to me that the
very same thing has been done by the department before under the Indian Act, and that is why I am asking the minister what is [DOT] the necessity for bringing in this bill.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: I am advised by the law officers of my department that the authority asked for under this bill is necessary to give us full control of these islands. We certainly would not ask for this special bill if we had authority under the general act.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Consent of superintendent required for occupation, etc.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: Surely the department has the right under the general act to make regulations such as those described in this section to prevent any person going on Indian land and cutting down and carrying away trees.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Of course,
no one could do so without being subject to action for trespass, but we are simply making the position clear with respect to these islands. The clause may not be entirely necessary, but I see no harm in it.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
There is a bill
now before the House for the amendment of the general act. I take, it for granted that under the general act the department has 
power to make regulations in the terms of section 3 of this bill. Therefore why the department should be given this power in a special bill is something that I cannot understand. It seems to me that if the department is not satisfied with the general act as it stands in dealing with these and other Indian islands, the minister had better suggest amendments that his officials consider necessary.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
I think it
is only fair where you are taking absolute control over certain lands that you should designate those lands in a separate piece of leigislation. We have general powers for leasing, but we have not power under the Indian Act to take absolute control of any Indian land on behalf of the department. That is what we are seeking to get here.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: But do not those general powers cover what you are seeking under section 3?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
Powers are
delegated under the act to the council, subject to the approval of the superintendent general, but in this particular case we are taking power to deal absolutely with these lands, making provision not to dispose of them, but simply to lease them. We are also making regulations with respect to trespass and so forth. The control of the reserves under the Indian Act is primarily with the council, subject to the approval of the superintendent general.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: That is all right so far as section 2 is concerned, but as to section 3, the minister has not said whether the department has or has not now under the general act the power to make regulations bearing on that section.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
As I say,
the power is in the council, subject to the approval of the superintendent general.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
When shall the bill be
read the third time?

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
With the consent of the minister I would suggest that the bill remain in committee until we get some further explanation as to why we should have certain sections in this act instead of in the general act.

Indian Act

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext: If any remedy is necessary, the hon. member may have it on the third reading of the bill, unless he wishes to move now that the bill be referred back to the committee.

maintopic: ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE CONTROL OF ST. LAWRENCE ISLANDS BY SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL
speechtext:
With the consent of the minister I move that the House go into comimittee again on the bill.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Progress reported.

Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Edmonton, Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 56 to amend the Indian Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1

If capital1 does not exceed two thousand dollars.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is to
give us power to dispose of certain small sums of money belonging to the Indians. It applies chiefly to the Indians of British Columbia where there are approximately about 100 bands whose capital ranges from $9.17 to $2,000. The annual interest on such funds is negligible. Many of the bands consist of just a few members and in some instances there is no occasion for the disposal of money. The purpose of the proposed amendment is to enable the Governor in Council to dispose of small amounts among the Indians in any way that may be deemed beneficial to them. When the amount involved is under $2,000 the distribution of interest entails a great deal of bookkeeping inasmuch as the individual member of the band receives so very small an amount. We are asking for authority to distribute these moneys amongst the bands interested and so clean up the situation.

That is, to distribute
the capital itself?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Are these small accounts stationary?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They are
capital accounts.
But not accounts that may be added to by some unexpected lease or sale of timber or land or some other resource on the reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No. In
that case there might be a possibility of the capital exceeding $2,000, but this is to fix an arbitrary amount from which point to work down to zero. It does not contemplate cases in which the capital amount may be augmented by subsequent sales.
That is the point.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The object
is to get rid of little capital accounts.
If these are dead accounts it is all right.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Regulations.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is to
give us more power over the operations of poolrooms, dance halls and places of amusement generally. In some instances we have no authority in relation to such matters, particularly as regards the sale of liquor on the reserves.

In my constituency is at
least a portion of the Six Nations Indians, who stand in a different class altogether from all other Indians in Canada. I am not competent to give the complete history of the Six Nations Indians, but the committee will remember that during the Revolutionary war in the United States these Indians were allies of the British nation, and remained loyal. After the war they, like a number of others, were excluded from the American nation and forced to leave that country,, as were the United Empire Loyalists. These Indians came to Canada under a treaty with King George which allowed them certain rights in this country. In intelligence the Six Nations Indians compare very favourably indeed with the average white man; the average Indian in the townships of Tuscarora and Oneida is quite equal to the average white man, and is quite capable of managing his own affairs. Therefore I think there should be an exception made in the case of those Indians known generally as the Six Nations. I do not know whether they should be under the Indian act at all; they were brought here by the British government and given certain lands under the Haldimand treaty, with which I am not familiar, I do know, however, that these lands were largely reduced by subsequent treaties.
Indian Act

I do not know how these later treaties were made; I have a question on the order paper in that connection which will give that information. Originally the Six Nations were entitled to a strip of land six miles wide from the mouth to the source of the Grand river, and that has been reduced until now they are in two townships, one in the county of Brant and the other in the county of Haldimand. The government still assumes to deal with these lands; they are held under life leases or in some other way with which I am not familiar, but as I have already said these Indians are thoroughly capable and well-behaved citizens of Canada, and I do not think the Indian department should longer assume the position of superiority implied by the Indian act. I would ask the minister if he will not take into consideration the question of excepting the Six Nations Indians from the provisions of the bill now before the House.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I inherited
the responsibility of dealing with the Six Nations Indians as well as all other Indians in Canada. Of course where an Indian becomes enfranchised and takes upon himself the responsibility of full citizenship, he is no longer upon the reserve. I do not desire to discuss the treaty respecting these Indians; I understand my hon. friend is asking a question which will bring the matter up. I am not prepared to discuss that matter to-day nor am I ready to give a direct answer as to whether I would advise the release of the Six Nations Indians from the control of the Indian act. For one thing, I might say that there is a very serious difference of opinion between the bands themselves on that reserve, not through any interference by the Indian department but because of a difference in their own ideas. Just whether or not these Indians are at a stage of development where they can take full responsibility for their own affairs I am not prepared to say. White people quarrel amongst themselves and I see no reason why the Indians should not be 'given that privilege if they desire it. I may say, however, that this act applies to all the Indians in Canada; under section 92 the superintendent general may do a great many things, subject always to the councils selected by the Indians themselves, whose business it is to work under this act for the good government of their reserves. They themselves are desirous of having more stringent regulations governing the licensing of pool halls, dance halls and other places of amusement on the reserves. In the bill there are a great many clauses enumerated having to do with sanitary regulations, regulations for taxation, the con-

trol and destruction of dogs destroying sheep and all that sort or thing. The council administers these by-laws in running the reserve, and this amendment simply asks for more control over the pool halls and other places of amusement.

The pool rooms and dance
halls and places of that character are taxed by the provincial government; the pool rooms pay a flat rate and the dance halls pay amusement tax. Will that still be operative in this case?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No. The
Indian reserves are quite immune from any of the provisions of the provincial law. The control of the Indian reserves is under the jurisdiction of the federal government.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Life chiefs.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is
merely a change substituting the jurisdiction of the superintendent general for the Governor in Council. There is a restriction for three years, but if there is any protest I have no objection to dropping this.

There are two clauses
which substitute the superintendent general for the Governor in Council, and one thought occurs to me in that connection. After all, in dealing with the members of our Indian tribes, and remembering their position as related to our own and as related to the government, I think it desirable to keep them as closely identified with the government as we possibly can. In other words, I think we might accord them this distinction, that their removal must be by the Governor in Council. It is a small thing, and really I would suggest to the minister that these two clauses be dropped. I do not think there is much need for them and it is one of those little courtesies which I think will probably smooth the paths of the department and of the minister.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am not particularly keen about this; as a matter of fact I rather welcome the responsibility of the order in council, although of course the superintendent general must take the responsibility of recommending it.
It is very little trouble, just a pro forma order.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have no objection to dropping these two sections, and carrying on as we have done in the past.
Sections 3 and 4 dropped.

Ottawa Electric Company
On section 5-confirmation by the superintendent.

As to clause 5 I should
think the same thing would apply unless there is some reason for using the word "also".

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This clause is not so important, perhaps, as the other. The other dealt with the removal of the chief and councillors and head men. This is a matter which merely deals with regulations. To provide that there should be an order in council will give an air of greater authority.
I think so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have no
particular objection. The sole object was to simplify the administration, that is all we had in mind. But if there is a feeling that the matter should proceed by order in council I do not object.
That is more formal.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I move that section 5 be dropped.

Motion agreed to.
Section 6 agreed to.
On section 7-Acquisition of totem poles, etc., forbidden.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This clause applies particularly to British Columbia, and it is something that we are desirous of having, because these works of art, if one may call them such, are very rapidly disappearing on the coast.

There is only one thing
I should like to ask t'he minister. I am fully in accord with the idea expressed in this clause, but some of the Indians are making a business of carving small replicas of these totem poles and selling them, which I think is a very useful thing.	Would this clause prevent
them from doing that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is not our intention. We are seeking to preserve these totem poles because of their historic value.

It says here:
No title to any. . . carved grave pole, totem pole, carved house-boat, or large rock-
And so on. The clause as it now reads would include any carved thing of that character, would it not? I know some of the Indians, for example those around Alert bay, carve these replicas and sell them to the tourists that go by on the Alaska tourist steamship route. We have a small one in our own home that was given to us by an Indian.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There would be no objection to the Indians doing that, although, perhaps, the clause might be interpreted to mean that they would not have such a right. I do not know how we are going to take power to prevent the sale of these historic tribal relics without having this clause in the bill.
The language seems to be so sweeping in its character that I think it would have the effect of stopping 'this business to which I referred, although it is one which should be encouraged, I think.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I quite admit the force of my hon. friend's contention, but I do not know how we are going to have the necessary authority, unless we have some such clause.	1

Perhaps between now and
eight o'clock t'he minister may hit upon something which would overcome the difficulty.
Progress reported.

[DOT] .
On section 7-Acquisition of totem poles, etc., forbidden.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Our difficulty in connection with these totem poles, which are from fifteen to forty-five feet high, is that rich Americans have been coming up into British Columbia and purchasing them, and if this goes on the whole coast will soon be denuded of these totem poles if we do not take some action to preserve them. They are of great historic value. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre raised the question of Indians being allowed to practise the art of making miniature totem poles for sale. There is no objection in the world to that on the part of the department. The totem poles that we have in mind and wish to preserve are in the nature of stationary monuments, carvings on rocks, and the posts that appear along the coast. The art of making smaller totem poles would not be interefered with by this provision at all. This is merely to preserve the historic mementoes of the Indian tribes along the coast, and it applies only to British Columbia.
Have quite a number of these totem poles been sold?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, Americans have been purchasing them and taking them to the United States and placing them on their properties there. We want to preserve at least enough for those who come after us, or otherwise they will be found only in museums.

I notice that the clause
is not drafted to apply to sales, but only to removal. There is no prohibition against the sale.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The sale
would'not be valid; removal cannot take place.
There is nothing to make the sale valid. There is a provision to make the removal invalid. If a bona fide sale takes place, is the purchaser not entitled by law to remove what he has purchased?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It says:
No title. . . . shall be acquired by any means whatsoever by any person without the written consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.

The word "acquired"
would cover it.

I would like to point out
to the minister in charge of this bill while it is perhaps desirable to retain these historic poles, I do not see why we should interfere with the Indians engaging in the occupation of making new totem poles, which is getting to be quite an industry now, just as the manufacture of old furniture is becoming quite an industry. They are copies, and they do not profess to be anything else but what they are. Why should these people who have had this facility 'handed down to them through long years of tradition and practice be prevented from selling the work of their hands from day to day? A distinction should be drawn between the old historic totem poles and the copies. I fear this restriction will apply to all copies made an the future.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is not
the intention of the department that this should apply to those which are simply copies, but rather to the historic poles and monuments. They are taking the monuments as well as the poles, and anything that is a copy could be sold quite freely.
Not under this legislation.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is
just this one restriction. May I point out that unless we have this power, all will be sold. If you make distinctions, you will have difficulty in distinguishing between what is really a copy of the historic pole and what is the real article. I wish to assure the committee that there will be no objection in the world to the Indians carrying on the art of copying these monuments and historic poles.

The bill does not say so,
and I suppose it is the bill that will govern the Indian agent and the Indian department.

Indian Act

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend inserts a provision that the Indians may freely dispose of the copies without reference to the department, then in all probability the historic poles will go as well.

I would suggest that the
clause be worded so that no poles made previously to this shall be disposed of and any poles made subsequently to this may be disposed of by obtaining the consent of the Indian agent who is always immediately available, and who can put a stamp on it and permit it to be exposed for sale. As the bill stands now, while I quite understand there is no intention of doing what I am speaking about, the bill does not say so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If the Indian is permitted to dispose of copies without this restriction, without reference to any one, we shall have a great deal of difficulty in preserving the historic poles that are of value Even if you inserted in the bill a provision allowing the Indians to sell, the sale would have to be under the control of the department, because otherwise as these historic poles are almost invaluable to some people who have money to spend on articles of historic value, they will pay fabulous prices for them. Therefore it is simply an endeavour to preserve these poles of historic value, and if the Indian manufactures a new one and desires to sell it, such a sale can be very easily arranged for by the department.

The department will make
regulations to that effect?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

Then I would suggest that
the matter be made subject to the permission of the written consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, or anyone deputed by him. Otherwise every time an United States tourist wants to go ashore from a steamer and pay six bits for a little thing about six inches long, he has to get the written consent of the man down here at Ottawa There is no sense to that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This would not apply to the small copies. That is the very point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), but it is pointed out that they make exact copies of the poles that are from twenty to thirty feet high. I do not know whether they do or not.

Certainly they do.
32649-21i

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
What my
hon. friend was objecting to was in connection with these smaller copies of the originals that are sold every day by these Indians who are practising their art. There is no interference with that at all.
The bill says that they have to send to the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, and he is three thousand miles away. It will take a month or six weeks to get his consent.

I presume the
superintendent general would have power to delegate his consent in regard to small copies without reference to him on each particular occasion.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The consent in that case will be obtained from the superintendent who is located at Victoria.
The consent applies not to the copies but to the originals. Is it the intention of the department to allow these originals to be taken away?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The bill
does not say anything about originals or copies. It says simply that these monuments, poles, gravehouses, carved posts, shall not be disposed of without the consent of the department. That is the wording of the bill.

That is hardly a fair statement. It says that they must not be disposed of without the written consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. If it was the department I would not have much objection, -because that consent would be obtained from the agent who is available in time, perhaps in three weeks. The bill does not say that; it says "without the written consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs", and there is only one man in that position. It does not say any one deputed by him. So when the United States tourist comes along from the steamer-and he is an important source of revenue to members of these bands -and says: "I will give you $75 for that totem pole", the man says "All right. Sit down and write a letter to Ottawa and you will get an answer back in the course of six weeks, when we shall be able to make a deal". I am not going to press the matter further, but I know there will be a great deal of discontent. I know the object is desirable, but it could be attained in such a way as not to
Indian Act

hurt these Indians, many of whom make a living by carrying out this very art which we say is desirable and which soon they will be discouraged from carrying out if they find they cannot get a ready sale.

The hon. gentleman says that the object is to prevent these old historic marks from being disposed of. In that case it is a very proper thing that the written consent of the superintendent general should be had, because that would prevent their being disposed of.

My point is the delay occasioned in writing to Ottawa to get the written consent. The United States tourist is not going to wait while you write to Ottawa, three thousand miles away, for the written consent.
The object is to prevent their being sold at all.
I am talking about the copies.
I would not say that this applies to the copies.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not
think so. Of course lawyers can make these things apply to anything, but that is not really the intention. The intention is to preserve these historic monuments. '

I will not delay the minister beyond one suggestion. I would suggest that in line 20, instead of saying:
Without the written consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.
Put:
Without the authority of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.
Then the minister by regulation can authorize the local agents to supervise the matter.

It would be well to define what is meant by the term " totem pole ". Is that .the original pole owned by the tribe or one of the very many representations of it that are made annually? On my annual trips up and down the coast I see so-called totem poles manufactured and sold by the cord, not only to United States tourists, but to all classes of tourists. Has any one of these Indian carpenters who carves out a totem pole, before he makes a sale, to get leave from the Indian department? Surely that is not the intention. These are merely copies. It seems to me it is hardly necessary that any legislation should be passed to prevent these people from selling these carved objects any more than that they should get leave from the Indian department to sell a wicker basket.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have just been trying to point out to the committee that if you give the Indians the privilege of selling exact copies of the totem poles you will have veiry great difficulty in preventing sales of .the originals and they will disappear entirely. This provision may appear to work a hardship on the Indians, but strong representations have been made to us that these monuments are of great historic value not only from the standpoint of the people of British Ccftumbia but from the standpoint of the Indians themselves. We cannot enforce an authority such as that suggested by my hon. friend, and I think on further consideration he will realize this. There is a tremendous territory to guard and there are still some very valuable historic poles to be found there.
Why not specially provide for totem poles of historic value?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If you give permission for the sale of copies you cannot very well guard the historic poles, for they will be more valuable and more eagerly sought after than the copies, with the resdlt that somebody will arrange to get the originals out of the country. True, this section provides that we may seize any article removed, but we cannot very well recover a totem pole taken into the United States, for instance. If there is any desire on the part of the people of British Columbia who made these representations to preserve these historic monuments, then we must have control over the copy as well as over the original itself.

Section agreed to.
Section 8 agreed to.
On section 9-Receiving money for the prosecution of a claim.
Mr. MoPHERSON: Mr. Chairman, there might perhaps be occasions when the minister would not want this section to be enforced. I can personally recall two or three instances when a considerable sum of money was obtained for the Indians of Manitoba from the American government. We have a situation there that is perhaps unique, in that a large tend of Sioux Indians came over from the States immediately after the Custer massacre and settled near Portage la Prairie. I know that during the past two years they have received from $3,000 to $10,000 from the American government. I do not know what legal charges were made for obtaining payment of that money, but I do know the money was secured through the assistance of solicitors. Under this clause those solicitors would be prosecuted. I do not think that is

Agricultural Winter Fair
quite right, nor do I think it necessary that a solicitor in such a case should have to apply to the superintendent general for permission to act. I may add that there is more money coming to those Indians, because they have in the United States a rather valuable territory. I would suggest that the section should receive further consideration.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is exactly why we want this clause -in order that we -may exercise some supervision over persons who make private bargains with Indian bands for the purpose of collecting claims, whether legitimate or imaginary. I do -not like to mention names, but a case has come to my notice since I have been Superintendent General of Indian Affairs in relation to a very large claim which we think is owing by the American government to a band of Indians located in Ontario. Notwithstanding that the department has spent considerable sums of money in securing advice as to the possibility of collecting the claim, this band made a solemn agreement) with an attorney under which he was to be remunerated for his services at the rate of nearly fifty per cent of whatever moneys might be collected by him. I could cite a dozen other instances in which representations were made to Indians with respect to certain claims, for the collection of which the Indians agreed to pay substantial remuneration. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) would not have to go very far to cite one case-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: - in which for years the British Columbia Indians have been paying certain persons for their services in connection with claims which it had been represented could be enforced. I think those Indians -have claims-at all events for consideration. But from one end of Canada to the other it is becoming a common practice to represent to the Indians that they have certain rights, and those making the representations usually manage to get the Indians to enter into a contract providing substantial remuneration for their advisers. We think it is to the advantage of the Indians that these contracts should be scrutinized by the department in -order to protect them from exploitation.

Section agreed to.
Section 10 agreed to.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA

speechtext:
Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved. 1. That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the granting of financial assistance to the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair Association of Canada, for the purpose of erecting and equipping a building or buildings in the Exhibition park at Toronto, to be used to display for public inspection the live stock, agricultural and dairy products of Canada.
2.	That for the said purpose the sum of $35,000 each year for a period of twenty years, commencing with the fiscal year ending March 31, 1928, shall be paid out of the vote appropriated for "live stock, including exhibitions";
3.	That such grants shall be payable on condition that the government of the province of Ontario make to this association a grant equal in amount and for the same periods as the grants from the Dominion government, and upon such other conditions as to allocation of space, premiums, and plans and specifications, as may be prescribed.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
The primary purpose of this resolution, upon which a bill will be based, is to extend further assistance and encouragement to the live stock industry of Canada by making the definite grant stipulated in the resolution to the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair Association whose headquarters are located at the exhibition park in Toronto. We are dealing with the Royal association as well as with the live stock associations throughout Canada, and perhaps I may say a word in reference to the extensive building used at present and which has been in use for the past five years. About six or seven years ago-I think in 1921-the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair Association entered into an arrangement with the city of Toronto for the construction of a building costing $1,500,000 for the housing of the exhibits of that show. The show was increasing in proportions and the city of Toronto undertook to construct the present building, which was opened in 1922. The exhibits very soon became so numerous and the fair was so popular, being patronized from one end of the country to the other, that the building in 1923 proved1 quite inadequate to take care of all that was offered for display. In that year the building, although it covers five acres of ground space, was able to accommodate only about one third of the cattle exhibited, and all the poultry, leaving two-thirds of the cattle exhibits, all the horses, sheep and swine to be taken care of in temporary buildings
Agricultural Winter Fair

which were quite unfit for the housing of this high grade live, stock, most of which is pure bred.
The question then came up as to who would supply the additional housing accommodation which was found to be necessary. The exhibition had become not only of national but of international importance, attracting a large number of exhibits from the United States, just as the Chicago International Exhibition at-ti'acts exhibits from Canada. The association discussed the matter with the city of Toronto and the city took the ground that they had done as well as they could be expected to do, as in fact they have. They had risked their money and their judgment in putting up a building at a cost of a million and a half, believing that circumstances would justify that expenditure, and' that the exhibition would soon grow to the capacity of the building. Their belief was fully justified, for inside of two years the accommodation originally provided was found to be inadequate. The question is, should the further accommodation be provided by the province of Ontario, whose live stock men, to a greater extent possibly than those in other parts of Canada, enjoy the use of the building; or should the Dominion as a whole share in the expense? It must not be forgotten that live stock men throughout the country, from the maritimes to the Pacific, share in the accommodation afforded by the building. Should this parliament, therefore, assist in providing the necessary extension in conjunction with Ontario? The live stock men and the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair Association have agreed that it should, and have accordingly requested the government to take steps towards this end. Some two years ago we were asked to provide the necessary housing accommodation for this rapidly extending exhibition.
The resolution provides for an annual grant to the association of $35,000 for a period of twenty years. The legislature of Ontario has passed an act for a similar purpose, with the proviso that the Dominion should contribute its quota. We have agreed to do so on the same understanding. So that we have the three parties co-operating, the city of Toronto, which put up the original building at l cost, as I have said, of $1,500,000, and the province of Ontario and the Dominion government providing funds for the necessary extension on a fifty-fifty basis to the extent of $1,400,000. The building, when teomple/ted, will cover seven acres, and it is expected to oope fully with the demands. I may anticipate the question-why Toronto?
(Mr. Motherwell.]

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
No one has
asked it.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Well, one might say that Toronto has a record of a half century behind it of putting on one of the
best exhibitions in Canada and that it was to that city's own interest to put up the original building. But the question is, should Toronto be expected to accommodate this broad Dominion's live stock, or should the federal treasury assist with a small annual grant extending, as suggested, over twenty years, to help the province? If we Contribute, I canj assure the committee that (at the end of a very short time the entire accommodation will Ibe taken up by the exhibition, and then we shall have the most outstanding international live stock show on this continent.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: If this resolution passes, is the minister prepared to guarantee that, should other cities apply for similar assistance-say, Winnipeg, or as someone behind me suggests, Oallgary-that assistance will be given? This grant of $700,000 wail, with interest, run well up into a million.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: This includes the interest.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
I did not know
that. At any rate the money is intended to extend what after all, is a local exhibition. It is called "Royal" but I do not know what that means. We were told1 a year or two ago that it was against the law to attach this name to any private institution. Further than that, we are told that it was called the Winter Fair Association of Canada. I do not know why one particular city or province should undertake to call its local exhibition a Canadian exhibition. There are a great many other places which might do that equally well. It would seem to me that essentially this is a local exhibition; undoubtedly it has been successful in the past and I do not see why it should not continue its successful career. But if the government continues to make grants to one particular locality, we should have an assurance from the government that grants on a proportionate scale will be made to other parts of Canada.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
There is something in what my friend has said, but we will have to deal with each case as it comes before us.
I do not think we could undertake to 'have three or four outstanding national or international fairs or exhibitions in Canada at

Agricultural Winter Fair
this time, because we must have a reasonable amount of provincial co-operation before we can even have one good show, because of the scattered nature of our provinces. In the United States they concentrate on one outstanding international exhibition at Chicago; it is the centre of attraction of the whole continent, and I think most of us have the idea that we should also centre on one, but of course not altogether to the exclusion of all others. This government is giving more money to our exhibitions in Canada to-day than any other government in our history. In regard to Winnipeg, I may say that we have an allocation of what we call our "A" fairs; two of these have been allocated to each of the four western provinces but Manitoba only avails itself of one, because Winnipeg has not revived the exhibition which was formerly such a pronounced success. We are keeping a little niche in our program, however, looking to the day when the city of Winnipeg will once more conduct this fair and, by making use of the old grounds and renovating the old buildings, resume her place in the agricultural life of Manitoba. If Winnipeg does that the usual grant given "A" fairs will be made, but outside of that I cannot say anything further, except that I think at this juncture we should confine ourselves to the idea of one outstanding national exhibition, and then deal with other applications on their merits.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Is it not a
fact that the Toronto exhibition is the only exhibition carried on in the Dominion of Canada which has the right to be called international at present?

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: I think so.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
If you are
going to make this apply to side shows in Winnipeg and other places like that where they gather a few people together for a visit once a year or once every two or three years, the next thing will be applications from every township for the little one-day shows. The only reason back of this grant is the fact that this exhibition is international.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
That is its only
justification.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: It is international, and when the city of Winnipeg or any other city in Canada can establish a fair of anything near the proportions of the Toronto exhibition I dare say this parliament will be ready to take that into consideration, and it would be in the general interests of Canada to do so. But there is no comparison at all between a grant for a little show in Winnipeg and a grant for the international exhibition in Toronto.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has .confused two things; the exhibition at Toronto is not being discussed. We were discussing the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair, an exhibition for the display of the live stock, agricultural and dairy products of Canada. If the point under discussion were the relative merits of the Toronto exhibition and any western exhibition I think possibly my friend's observations, in a little different language, might be well taken, but while we in the west have not the population of the east, we do not conduct exhibitions as side shows. That must be clearly understood, because the winter exhibitions of live stock in western Canada are international in their character, as the minister very well knows; he also knows the efforts now being made to centralize these exhibitions in the city of Winnipeg this winter. I believe those efforts will be successful, because a large convention is being held in Winnipeg within the next few weeks, if I remember correctly. I know that on one occasion this parliament was good enough to vote a very large sum to Calgary to assist the exhibition there. So I would very much regret anyone giving voice to the thought in this chamber that the cattle of eastern Canada and the dairy and agricultural products of eastern Canada are in any sense better than those of the west. The population of western Canada is very much less than that of the east, but having regard to the population it is only fair to say that western cattle have taken first prizes in every part of the world where they have been exhibited; the same may be said with respect to sheep and horses, to a lesser extent, while our dairy products really form the basis of the largest export trade in dairy products which we have at present. So I would like the House to realize that it is not voting money for the great Toronto exhibition, which is international in its character, but for a cattle exhibition in the city of Toronto, a winter show for cattle and dairy products. To that extent I hope the day is not far distant when under similar conditions we may be able to make some similar appeal for one of the cities in western Canada.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
It is quite
true that this amount is for the winter exhibition, but there is a relation between the winter exhibition and the international exhibition which .must be remembered. I venture to say that this application would never be considered for a moment if it were not for that relationship.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Agricultural Winter Fair

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
My hon.
friend was very bard up for an argument when he took the ground that I intimated that the cattle of western Canada were not equal to those of the east; I did not suggest that for one moment. This is not an exhibition for Ontario cattle; cattle from western Canada will be on exhibition there as well as eattle from other parts of Canada and from the United States. II repeat that there is a connection between this winter show and the international exhibition, and if it were not for the fame that exhibition has acquired all over the world this grant would not have been asked for and would not have been made.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
I hope the
committee will not lose too much time in discussing this item which the good minister has recommended. Every one knows that this is not a local fair or a local association of any kind. The live stock associations of Canada are all interested in this coliseum which it is proposed to build; as the minister said, the city of Toronto spent a million and a quarter to build the coliseum already there, which to-day will not house more than one-third or one-half of the exhibits entered. These exhibits come from the west, from every province of Canada and from almost every state in the union. This is an international fair pure and simple, and I hope the vote will go through without any further discussion which only leads to more controversy.
Mr. C'OOTE: I am very sorry to disappoint any hon. member for Toronto by not letting this amount go through without further discussion, but I am afraid it cannot be helped. I would suggest to the minister that the time to cut out these dips into the treasury, which he described so realistically, is right now before we make this grant to the royal winter fair at Toronto. He is starting out on a policy that will, I am sure, lead his government and successive governments into trouble. Since the minister assumed charge of the department he has been cutting down grants to fairs, starting with the little fairs. There is too much concentration in Toronto. There are enough things centralized in that city now without handing that city a grant of $700,000 to put up another building. They have got lots of money in Toronto to put up such a building; most of the money in Canada is corralled in that City. It would not hurt the citizens of Toronto very much to pay $700,000 themselves to put up this building if they needed it. The thing is wrong in principle. If you want a place for a central exhibition in Canada, that place surely is Winnipeg,

because it is nearer the centre of Canada than Toronto. In the years to come it is certainly going to be the centre of Canada as far as agricultural production is concerned, and dairy products at that. I do not think the minister has really given us any very good reason for embarking on a policy of subsidizing this exhibition association in order to enable them to put up a building. The minister has been hard enough on the small fairs by cutting down their grants, but he still continues to make grants to the bigger associations. I think that while he is doing that, this association should take care of its own buildings. I do not think this government, or this House should embark on a policy of putting up buildings for exhibition associations.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman who preceded me cannot be serious. If he is, he is speaking without regard to the facts. The hon. gentleman must know that we are not making a grant to the city of Toronto. The exhibition of the royal winter fair is held in Toronto, but it is not in the interest of the city of Toronto but of the whole Dominion. Toronto is capable of looking after its own fairs and does not need to ask for anything here. What is more if it did I do not believe the Minister of Agriculture would grant it.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
The last speaker
is quite right. This proposition is to provide for the housing of the pure bred live stock of Canada and not to house the pure bred Tories of Toronto. The city of Toronto has demonstrated for many years its capacity for putting on and pulling off excellent exhibitions. It is a large, populous centre, with good hotels and good railway connections, and it is the centre to which the live stock of all Canada are gravitating. Every provincial government helps to pay the freight bill of the respective-provincial exhibits to this great national exhibition, so that it has the sympathetic support of all the provinces of Canada. I hope my hon. friend from Macleod will endeavour to take a broad, national aspect of this undertaking, and forget that there is such a place as Toronto. Let him remember the needs of the live stock industry. This building must be located somewhere, but if anybody can find a better place than Toronto I will consider the proposition. In the absence of any better location it seems to me that Toronto is the logical place.
Now as to the necessity of this accommodation, the matter has been fought out for the last three years. The exhibits are so crowded that exhibitors are considering the idea of

Agricultural Winter Fair
discontinuing sending them because there is not proper accommodation. In the weather such as we have in November, the ground is simply nothing but a quagmire. There is such a demand for accommodation that temporary buildings, even tents, have to be provided, and for the exhibition of horses recourse has been had to box cars. While the judges are at work the horses are taken out of the cars, and then returned again to the restricted accommodation which (those cars offer. That cannot continue. The exhibition must go forward and develop in accordance with its possibilities as a great national show. It cannot be expected that in a case of this kind the whole burden should be supported by Toronto; some of it must devolve upon the rest of the Dominion.
Mr. CO'OTE:	I should like the minister
and the people of Toronto as well to understand clearly that I am not objecting to this grant because it is going to Toronto. I am objecting to it simply because I think it is wrong in principle and because I think we should not embark upon such a policy. The minister seems to argue that the building should be provided because the exhibits have been increased. In that case if Calgary wanted a new building all its people would have to do would be to come down to the minister and say, "We have got to house some live stock in box cars and we should like to have $700,000 in order to make an addition to our building." I would not object if the government or the minister think they have plenty of money for all these purposes; but when I have to pay about $2 in the shape of a tax on my sleeping car berth to the Dominion government when I want to come down to Ottawa, I think the government must be pretty hard up for money to run the country. Erecting exhibition buildings is a poor policy for us to embark on. Let me repeat to the hon. member (Mr. Spence), who resented my remarks, that I do not object to Toronto getting this grant simply because it is Toronto. I object to the principle contained in the policy we are embarking upon here of putting up buildings in which to hold winter fairs, or summer fairs either for that matter.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
As one of the
western members of this House I should like to take the opportunity of agreeing for once with my hon. friends from Toronto. The winter show in Toronto is a national show, and people come from all over the Dominion to compete. We are not giving Toronto, or the Toronto exhibition, anything in this grant; we are simply adding to the accommodation
for the annual exhibition of the winter fair so that a national show can be accommodated properly.

maintopic: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL WINTER FAIR ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: That is right.

speechtext:
To try to build
up a national show in any other part of Canada to-day would take three or four times the amount of money asked for in this vote, and unless we are going to allow the great live stock show of Canada to retrogress, we have got to spend a little money immediately.
