I wish to say a word in
support of this resolution, for one or two reasons. In the first place this winter show must not be regarded as a Toronto conception at all. I have perhaps occasion to be somewhat intimately connected with it for the reason that most of the men who are associated with it come from the constituency that I represent in this House. Have the members who suggested Winnipeg or Calgary as the scene of an exhibition men in their midst who would give as much time and energy to the building up of a show as Mr. John Bright, for example, who was the live stock commissioner for Canada for a great number of years, and to whom, I think, we may attribute the building of this coliseum and the establishment of this fair in Toronto? Mr. Robert Miller, who was president of the fair two years ago. and the present president of t(he fair, Mr. Dryden, are both from my constituency, and by virtue of that fact naturally they would expect me to say something in regard to this resolution. I consider that it is a move in the right direction, and I would say to the gentlemen from Winnipeg that if they would give as much time to the development of a show in Winnipeg as Mr. Miller, Mr. Dryden and Mr. John Bright have given to the development of this fair in Toronto, they would be justified in having a grant. I know that our people will be quite thankful for the efforts that are being put forward, because the accommodation is absolutely needed. I am very glad to support the resolution.

Old Age Pensions

Hon. PETER HEENAN (Minister of Labour) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a
measure respecting old age pensions, and to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council may make an agreement with the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of any province for the payment to such province quarterly of an amount equal to one-half of the net sum paid out during the preceding quarter by such province for pensions pursuant to a provincial statute authorizing and providing for the payment of such pensions to the persons and under the conditions hereinafter specified and regulations made under the proposed legislation.
2.	That every agreement so made shall continue in force so long as the provincial statute remains in operation or until after the expiration of ten years from the date upon which notice of an intention to determine the agreement is given by the Governor General to the Lieutenant-Governor of the province with which the same was made.
3.	That before any agreement so made comes into operation, the Governor in Council shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province, and no change in such scheme shall be made by the province without the consent of the Governor in Council.
4.	That all sums payable to any province in pursuance of any such agreement shall be payable from time to time on the certificate of the Minister of Finance out of any moneys belonging to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada not otherwise appropriated.
5.	That provision shall be made for the payment of a pension to every person who, at the date of the proposed commencement of the pension:

Mr. Chairman, I desire
to offer a word or two in regard to this resolution, more particularly to set clearly before the House the attitude of the Conservative party here, and I think of the Conservative party of Canada, in regard to the subject matter of the resolution; and I do so having regard to the debate which took place in this House on this question less than a year ago, which, of course, is found fully reported in Hansard.
Those who were present in the House when the former bill was introduced last session will remember quite clearly the discussion which took place. A great many members of the Conservative party in the House at that time spoke to this measure when it was in the committee stage. I have read over the debate with some care, and I think I can state with assurance that each hon. member on this side of the House who discussed the proposal on that occasion agreed as to the principle of the bill then submitted. They did not acce*t it as an ideal measure by any means, but rather took the view that it was better to accept half a loaf than no bread. Member after member on this side of the House criticised many of the details of the measure; our suggestions were met in very good spirit by the government at the time, and some most useful amendments were made to the bill as originally drawn.
Several members on this side of the House said very clearly, very ably, very forcibly, that while they were prepared to support the measure then submitted they would have preferred a much wider measure, one applying

Old Age Pensions
to the whole Dominion of Canada, rather than one conditional upon its acceptance by this province, that province and the other province, which was the proposal submitted by the government.
On behalf of the government it was urged in regard to the bill then presented, which was a sort of provincial arrangement, that in order to come within our constitutional rights in this House it was necessary that we should become practically subservient to the will of the provinces in this matter. Indeed, it was intimated on more than one occasion during the debate that this House had no constitutional right to pass an old age pension bill. Opinions were cited from some of the law officers of the Department of Justice, but the opinions cited did not bear out the contention of those hon. members who had urged that this House had not the inherent right to pass an old age pension bill if it so desired.
Another objection that was taken, and very forcibly taken, was that the government's proposal in regard to old age pensions was too limited. Some considered the age limit of seventy too high. Another criticism which had force was that the pension was not founded at all on the question of disability, either ordinary physical disability, or disability through blindness or the like. It was founded solely upon one consideration-old age, and old age did not count until one had reached the age of seventy years.
Old age and destitution.

I did not notice the word destitution. I assume that one must accompany the other. I think our position was made abundantly clear, Mr. Speaker, upon that question. It was deemed to be the unanimous wish that the bill should pass unchallenged after amendment and after discussion in the committee, and the bill did pass this House unchallenged; there was no division on it. But during the course of the election last fall I think I am safe in saying that in every quarter of Canada Conservative candidates in the various ridings: were charged with opposition to the old age pension bill. Upon almost every Liberal: platform that charge was made. I remember being in the city of Windsor during the last election and being handed an election card 'charging the present member from the city of Windsor with having voted against the old age pension bill. That is only one instance; but in riding after riding, it was charged against the Conservative party and Conservative candidates that they had opposed the passage of that bill through the House of Commons.
I am speaking at this moment in order to make our position absolutely clear upon this question. The position of the Conservative party in this House in regard to old age pensions as proposed in this measure is this. We prefer a federal scheme. We prefer a scheme which will apply equally to every corner of Canada. This bill is limited to those persons who are in destitution and who have reached the age of seventy years. Apply the proposal to the Dominion of Canada equally and let the Dominion treasury bear the expense. I say to my right hon. friend and his government:	If you will do
that, I believe you will have something in the nature of a real pension measure for the class of persons to whom it applies. I am not seeking in my present remarks to extend the measure beyond those described in this resolution, namely, those who are destitute and at the age of seventy; but taking that as the standard adopted by this government, I say:	Go further than you have gone;
make it an all Canadian scheme; adopt the federal principle and apply it throughout the whole Dominion. Then you will have a pension scheme which may and which will be of some advantage to the people who seek it.
My criticism of the present measure is just the criticism which was levelled against it last session. In all probability it will be inoperative. It is founded upon a wrong principle. We have in this confederation nine self-governing provinces. This proposal is based upon the theory that these provinces are going to agree to a measure dictated by the federal parliament. The federal parliament proposes a measure and says to each of the provinces: If you adopt this measure which we propose, then we will pay one-half of the amount that you are called upon to pay in respect of pensions to aged people. That is an improper principle. It is nothing short of dictation to the provincial governments of this country.
But what is the actual situation? Last session there was only a very faint intimation that any single province would come into the scheme. Member after member on this side of the House urged that the provinces be called together in conference to say what their attitude was in regard to this proposal. But no, the government would not hear of such a suggestion. They wanted to go boldly forward and practically say to the provinces of Canada: There is the measure; we dictate its terms; come in or stay out. What will happen if some of the provinces stay out? Supposing Ontario or Quebec decides not to come in under the present proposal, what will be the result? Other
Old Age Pensions

provinces may come in, and Ontario or Quebec, refusing to come in, must bear their proportionate share of the taxation under a scheme with which they will have nothing to do. Does that not sound a little like dictation to the provinces of this Dominion? Is that not an imposition upon the rights of the people of the various provinces? That was one of the grounds upon which we argued that your measure was faulty; that in all human probability it would never have any results; that there had been no preparation for the proposal. Indeed I doubt if any progress has yet been made in regard to obtaining the views of the various provincial governments. It has been intimated that British Columbia is now likely to agree to the proposal at present before the House, but has the government any official assurance from any other province that it is likely to come into this scheme? If it has not, I tell my right hon. friend and his government that they are wasting the time of the House in proposing this measure. They will fool the people of this country who are depending upon obtaining old age pensions at some time in the not too remote future. If your bill passes, it may become absolutely inoperative.
Have we or have we not the right to pass a federal measure dealing with this matter? I submit without hesitation, without any reservation, that under the constitution of this country this parliament can pass a federal measure. Unquestionably it has the right, and if the government will propose a measure applying to all Canada, where the whole amount is to be paid out of the federal treasury, there can be no doubt as to our constitutional authority to do so. We impose no burden upon any province. We exact no condition from any province. We ask no contribution from any citizen of any province. We invade in no respect what is known as property and civil rights in the various provinces. We have the right. The only question is: I3 the government willing to exercise that right and pass a measure which will give relief to the people mentioned in this resolution and who, I submit, will receive no relief, or very tardy relief, if the present scheme is adopted by this parliament.
I wonder if the government has considered just what the scheme means to some of the provinces. I was startled by figures which I saw to-night. This proposal involves this, that if the provinces enter into it and pass legislation practically identical with the resolution which we are now discussing, they may ask for and receive from the federal treasury one-half the amount that they are called upon

to pay for the aged poor of their various provinces. I am going to take only the single instance of Nova Scotia. An estimate has been made of those in that province who are over seventy years of age, and it is said that forty per cent of those people will be able to qualify under this clause as destitute and also as having attained that age. Does the government realize what they are imposing upon Nova Scotia? They are asking that province to contribute, in addition to what they now contribute for their aged and infirm, some $600,000 or $700,000 per annum to carry out this measure. While the Duncan report, which we hope will give some relief, suggests an additional subsidy of only $850,000 all told for that province, if this government carries out its present proposal and Nova Scotia accepts it, almost the whole of that increased subsidy will have to be paid out for old age pensions. I do not know what the figures are in regard to the other provinces. I have seen them in tabulated form, but the one that struck me was with regard to Nova Scotia. That is a burden which that province cannot bear.
I object to this scheme as a mere piece of patchwork. One of the chief criticisms to be levelled1 against it is that it will apply unequally, bear unequally, unless every province submits to the dictation of this government in matters over which they themselves have control. Now, have I made clear the position of the party which I have the honour to represent in this House upon this question? We ask for a federal measure. The cost of the present proposal is estimated at something like $12,000,000 a year. The cost of a federal scheme, according to the report of the committee which examined into these matters, would be about $23,000,000 a year. Shall we make two bites of the cherry, I ask? Why not adopt a federal scheme? Why not pay the whole amount out of the federal treasury in order that we may have a uniform system throughout Canada?-one which must bear equally upon all the provinces, because all the provinces must contribute their fair proportion of the taxation of the country.
That is the policy of the Conservative party on the subject. That is the measure for which we ask. If it is denied to us, what are we to do? Vote against the present measure? No. We will do as we did last session, we will say to the government and to the country: We will accept half a loaf or a quarter loaf rather than get no bread at all, and our support of the present bill is only by reason of the fact that this government will not bring in a federal measure, which is the one we desire and the one we advocate.

Old Age Pensions

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to hear the remarks of the leader of the opposition, for if he is keen to spend $24,000,000 I am sure there will be a fair chance of getting him to vote for the $12,000,000 which we propose. As to the attitude of the Conservative party, I notice it is somewhat changed from that taken last session.
No.
I think there is on record a document from the then leader of the opposition to the effect that he would not consider the introduction of an old age pension plan for Canada.
I never heard of it.
Where is the document?
Will my hon. friend tell us what document he refers to? I have never heard of it. I am only asking out of curiosity now.

Before the debate is over I think the document will be produced, or I am very much mistaken. If it is not produced I will take back that statement. Referring to another remark by my hon. friend, I think he said that last session every member of the opposition spoke in favour of the principle of old age pensions. Well, I sat through nearly all the debate, and it may be I do not quite understand the English language, but I thought many members on the other side of the House were not only trying to discourage the adoption of an old age pension plan, but spoke absolutely against it. Indeed I do not think my hon. friend would have very far to look to find some around him right now.
I have read the debate.
You had better name them.

The argument of my hon. friend that the provinces would not co-operate in an old age pensions scheme is something like the argument that was advanced during the time when other co-operative measures were under consideration in this House, yet we find in operation to-day co-operative plans between the various provinces and the federal government calling for an expenditure of over $65,000,000 from the federal treasury, and instead of the provinces trying to withdraw from those agreements they are asking for their extension.
Again, last session I heard the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) read the replies received from the premiers of the different provinces, and I believe he stated that not one of those premiers was in favour of the old age pension bill at that time.
Hear, hear.

I had not read over the documents at that time, but I have taken the trouble to do so since, and I am glad the hon. member says, "hear, hear", because evidently he has not changed his mind. I find that the Premier of New Brunswick stated:
While I feel that it would be a good thing-
That is not against it, is it?
While I feel it would be a good thing, yet it would be impossible for me to commit the province to any action in this matter at the present moment.
Is he for it?
He endorses the principle.
But he would not commit the province to it.	[DOT]

As an example, the province of British Columbia was opposed to this scheme because the obstacles in the way were insurmountable, but to-day we have the spectacle of a bill introduced in the legislature-
"Spectacle" is right.
-providing for this on a co-operative plan.
What about Quebec?

We will discuss the details when the bill is before the committee. From the information we have in the Department of Labour we fluid that there are many schemes of old age pensions, about twenty-eight in fact, some providing for pensions at the age of seventy, others at sixty-five, others again at sixty, while in other oases no age is specified; and others provide for a diminution of pensions if the pensioner bias an income or is possessed of property. In other words, it appears that old age pensions have been adopted in various countries to meet the conditions peculiar to those places.
In this country the subject of old age pensions has been under consideration for the past twenty years. In 1906 a resolution was introduced to deal with the matter, and again in 1908, in 1912 and in 1913, resolutions were introduced calling for the appointment of special committees to consider the advisability of adopting an old age pensions plan. In 1908 a law was passed authorizing the sale of annuities for old age. That was the first practical movement in the direction of bid age pensions ever made in Canada. In 1914 a resolution in favour of an old age pension system for this country was moved in the House, but the debate was not concluded. In 1922 the House of Commons adopted a resolution introduced by the member for Hull declaring that in its opinion the federal government should consider the advisaJbility of devising ways and means of establishing a system of old age pensions in Canada. In 1924 a special committee of the House was appointed on motion of the Prime Minister to inquire into an old age pensions scheme for Canada. That committee reported on July 1, 1924, submitting the following recommendations:
1. That an old age pension system be established at the earliest possible date for deserving indigent persons of seventy years of age and upwards.

Old Age Pensions
2.	That applicants for pension must be British subjects of at least twenty years' residence in Canada, or naturalized subjects of at least fifteen years' naturalization and twenty-five years' residence.
3.	That the maximum rate of pension be twenty dollars per month, which will be lessened by private income or partial ability to earn.
4.	That one-half of the amount of the pension payable be borne by the federal government; the other half, by the provincial governments of such provinces as express by legislation their desire to adopt the system-the cost of administration to be borne by the provincial governments.
The report of the committee was communicated to the provinces to ascertain their views in the matter. At the session of 1925 the committee was reappointed, and the correspondence between 'the various provinces was submitted to it for consideration. After careful deliberation, and having obtained advice from the Department of Justice, the committee again favoured the adoption of a co-operative system of old age pensions. The chairman of the committee in moving the adoption of its report on June 18, 1925, in the course of his remarks said:
This government has taken the initial step and we hope the matter will be proceeded with and prosecuted until it arrives at a successful conclusion in a co-operative movement between the federal government and the provincial governments.
As hon. members are aware, the government last session introduced a bill along the lines recommended by that committee, and it is practically the same measure I have the honour to introduce at this time. The bill introduced last year passed this House, as hon. gentlemen no doubt know.
In view of the fact that representations have been1 made from some quarters urging that a different system be adopted, that is to.say, a purely federal scheme, and one which my hon. friend on behalf of the Conservative party now also advocates, I desire to call the attention of the House to the fact that, when the resolution to concur in the recommendations of the committee was before the House in 1925, the committee having suggested a co-operative plan, an amendment was moved that the report be referred back to the committee with instructions to consider and report again upon a purely federal scheme. That amendment was voted down by 139 to 17 in this chamber. There is no question therefore that the decision of the House at that time was lagaindt a purely federal system. As I have already said, the House during the last session passed the bill, but it 'sras subsequently defeated in the Senate and consequently did not become law.
During the last election campaign the question of old age pensions was one of the matters which were most prominently before the electorate of Canada. One could hardly read a newspaper during that campaign without noting some refereqce to the desirability of establishing a system of old age pensions in this country. If we are to interpret the will of the electorate on that question in the way we usually interpret electoral decisions, there can be no question that the principle adopted in this bill was endorsed by the people of Canada.
During the debate last session some members advocated a contributory system. I believe the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) was one of those who espoused that scheme. But as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) pointed out at that time, practically every scheme of old age pensions in existence to-day began upon a non-contributory basis. They were all initiated at first as purely non-contributory plans. Like the Prime Minister, I feel that if we were establishing an old age pensions scheme with our younger people in view, I should myself be inclined to the contributory system. But having in mind the fact that we are facing a practical problem, and that we are legislating for our old pioneers, indigents, if you will, who have been unable through lack of opportunity or by reason of misfortune to provide for themselves, I think that the plan we are now proposing is the best one, at least for the time being. At the same time I hope to see the annuity system developed-
Hear, hear.

I trust my hon. friend will say " hear, hear " to what follows. I hope to see the annuity system developed into a broad scheme of social insurance. Of course it will be on a contributory plan, and I am hoping that it will also he in co-operation with the provinces. I have given a good deal of study and thought to the extension of the annuity system, and I see great prospects ahead for that scheme.
It has just been argued by the leader of the opposition that the provinces may not come into the scheme on a co-operative basis, and one of the reasons given is that it would be too expensive; the province of Nova Scotia was taken as an example. I am afraid those supporting that view have not considered the fact that the provinces and1 the municipalities bear the entire burden now, and by this legislation we are attempting to lighten that load by offering to contribute one-half of the cost.
Old Age Pensions

One is Charity and the
other is a pension.
It does not matter what you call it; you may re-christen the bill if you like, but we are offering to bear one-half of the cost which they bear at present.
It does not touch that.
Who is taking care of it?
The municipalities.

And the provinces, and if we do it in co-operation with the provinces we will be using the machinery already in existence. I want to point out just what the establishment of a federal old age .pension plan might cost, considering administration only. I sent telegrams to several of the provincial premiers, to which I have received two replies. I asked the cost of administering the Workmen's Compensation Act and the Mothers' Allowance Act and I will give the House the replies received from Ontario and British Columbia. For the last full year in Ontario the cost of administering the Workmen's Compensation Act was $277,936.16, and the cost of administering the Mothers' Allowance Act $73,516.73, or a total for Ontario of $351,452.89. In British Columbia the administration of the Workmen's Compensation Act cost $104,980 and the Mothers' Allowance Act $16,048, or practically half a million dollars for these two acts in the two provinces. We would practically duplicate that expenditure if we set up a federal scheme of this kind, so is it not better to work in co-operation with the provinces in order to lessen the cost of administration by using their own machinery?
I think there can be no question of the necessity for an old age pension scheme for indigents; for proof of that we have only to look about us. Right here in Ottawa the city is at present taking care of 641 people, many of whom do not belong here, which is one of the difficulties all through the country in relief work. Men become indigent and come into towns and cities for relief; the municipalities often feel that they are overburdened with their own indigents, and try to evade the responsibility of taking care of the outsiders. In that way the burden is not shared equally, nor are the people treated in the same way.
I am sure that if hon. members will only think it over they will realize that we should give a better assurance to the older people, the pioneers of this country who have not been so fortunate as some of the rest of us, that in their declining years we will not throw them on the scrap heap.

Old age and poverty combined plead their own case; there is no necessity for anyone to advocate their cause, but I feel that we should not evade our responsibility by saying that we would prefer another act and therefore will not support this scheme.
This bill passed the House last session after a great deal of discussion, but was defeated in the Senate. Subsequently it went out to the electors during the last campaign, and if there was one question discussed more than another, even more than the customs scandal, it was the old age pension scheme. I contend that the principle of this bill has been endorsed by the people. To those who still think that the provinces may not co-operate let me say that when other schemes of a co-operative nature were under consideration here it was predicted that the provinces would not participate in them, yet now we have some five or six co-operative schemes in force calling for an expenditure by this government of over $65,000,000. Just last week we had representatives of the different provinces asking that we extend our activity in connection with one of these schemes. Nova Scotia was represented, and I cannot believe that Nova Scotia would have any less regard for humanity than for its progress along material lines.
The argument advanced by my hon. friend on behalf of Nova Scotia seems to be taken from other arguments advanced in another chamber during last session, and I do not think the people of Nova Scotia would agree that over forty per cent of those over seventy years of age are indigent and unable to take care of themselves. That is a guess, as many other things which have been said in this chamber are guesses. What we should do is pass a bill and get it in working order, and then we can amend it according to the experience gained from practical knowledge.
When the workmen's compensation acts were introduced, many of us thought the compensation was not sufficient, and many protests against the pittances, as they were called, were made. But some of us in the front row were fighting to get the principle established, and one of the things I would like to see established in the interests of the working men of this country now is an old age pension bill. Let us get it into working order and then it can be amended as was done with the Mothers' Allowance Act, the Minimum Wage Act for women and girls and the Workmen's Compensation Act. Now, as I say, British Columbia has not only intimated its approval in correspondence from the prime minister, but a bill was introduced at this session of the legislature providing for

the making of an agreement between the government of that province and the federal government. So that we have made a start along the right line.
Having given a great deal of thought and study to the subject, and having taken every possible factor into consideration, I think we should adopt this measure, and the principle contained in it, as best suited to the needs of the country at the present moment. The bill will accomplish what it is intended to do. It will assist those in need who are over seventy years of age and have not been able to provide for themselves in their declining years.
I should like to see all the members of the House range themselves unitedly behind this bill. Then we could impress everybody outside parliament who may have to deal with the subject in a legislative way that we are united in the matter. It will be a cue upon which they can act so that the law will be applied throughout the whole of Canada. After the measure has gone into effect and we find that any amendment is necessary, and the country is willing to support the obligation the change may involve, we can amend it just as we have amended other measures in the light of practical experience.

I do not think this House
needs any particular advocacy of an old age pension bill, and that part of the address of the Minister of Labour might very well have been omitted. My hon. friend has given a very lucid description of the difficulties which have arisen in endeavouring to secure the cooperation of the provinces in this measure. And whether he intended it or not he succeeded in convincing me that the federal government has not nearly approximated to that agreement with the different provinces which must be arrived at before this measure can be of any avail.
The position enunciated to-night by the hon. leader of the opposition is no new position for the Conservative party; it is the position that we on this side took when the bill came up for discussion in the House last year. I can refer to a speech of mine on that occasion, which was agreed to by all members on this side, which stated the position then as the leader of the opposition has stated it to-night.
At what page is it to be found?

At page 2495 of the revised
edition of Hansard. The quotation in question is:	* *
There is no legal objection to the passing of a bill by the federal House assuming the entire responsibility.

I am interpolating some words:
If the government feels it can go the whole way and provide the money for the scheme throughout the Dominion of Canada, I shall be very glad. Failing that, and in the hope of getting something, in the hope that the Prime Minister may prove to be right when he says that he is sanguine that it may lead to results, I shall support the measure.
Now that was a very definite agreement with the measure that was submitted, and members on this side of the House unanimously took that same position. Therefore there was never any question as to this side being opposed to the old age pension scheme on principle. We agreed to the measure. There was no vote against it. There was no suggestion of a vote against it. There was only the suggestion that it was a poor measure, inasmuch as it would not produce the result aimed at, but that if the government would consent to take all the responsibility on behalf of the Dominion, then we would get a bill that would be workable. I would like to answer a few of the criticisms made in reference to this resolution for fear that it may be criticized to death, as was done last year, or so damned with faint praise as to be ineffective. I would like first to deal with the remarks of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), who quoted a number of letters received from the different provinces, nearly all of which were unfavourable to the idea of co-operating with the federal government in an old age pension scheme. But he did not tell the situation and the circumstances. He and I were on a committee of this House in 1924 when this question was taken up and we decided that the first thing to do was to put it up to the provinces. We assumed that they knew what we thought we knew, that it was a provincial matter, but we had no authority to say so and we asked their opinion on that occasion. In response to that request we received the letters which the hon. member read and which, as he said, were all more or less antagonistic. I think the province of British Columbia went further than any of the others, practically telling us to mind our own business and attend tc our own affairs. Then the matter was referred to the same committee, in 1925 and we were attracted by the trend of thought which seemed to be prevalent, that it was our funeral and none of the business of the provinces, so we decided to ascertain whether we had been wrong. In doing so we obtained an opinion from several of the best law officers of the crown, gentlemen who are supposed to be expert and who had the experience acquired in previous questions to guide them. Their report was made in writing and is on record, and it stated emphatically that so far as the British North America Act was concerned this matter had nothing to do with the Dominion, but was entirely a matter for the provinces.

They did add a corollary to the effect that if this House chose to do so it could aid any scheme initiated by the provinces, but they stated emphatically that we could not pass an act containing anything of an obligatory character. So we found that our previous conviction was right, and that the conviction so pronouncedly held by the provinces was wrong. We then sent out another circular or round robin to the provinces, conveying the report of those law officers, and then found the situation entirely changed. Instead of finding that we were trying to shove some of our obligations on them, a thing they naturally resented, the provinces found on the contrary that the obligation was entirely theirs and that we were trying to help the thing along by giving half or nearly half of the cost if they would take up the scheme. It was then that the provinces took a different view and modified the position which they had previously taken. For instance, we find British Columbia writing to say that they now understood the situation in a different light, and further evidence of that fact is to be found when we note that just a few days ago the legislature of British Columbia unanimously passed the second reading of a bill accepting any bill which this parliament may pass along the line of that now before us. That is a very decided change of attitude from that expressed a couple of years before, when we were practically told to mind our own affairs.

Speaking from memory, we asked them in general terms What was the jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion in connection with support for destitute old age. Here is the answer:
The subject of old age pensions does not fall specifically within any of the enumerated subjects given to the Dominion under section 91 of the British North America Act, but does fall within the subject of property and civil rights committed to the provinces under section 92.
And then the Deputy Minister of Justice added this:
I am of the opinion that the subject matter of pensions has been entrusted to the provincial legislature rather than to parliament. I do not mean to suggest that parliament has not the power to legislate upon the subject so as to assist-
Mark that.

so as to assist the provinces or to establish an independent voluntary scheme, provided that in either case the legislation does not trench up on the subject matter of property and civil rights in the province, as, for example, by obligating any province or person to contribute to the scheme.
Old Age Pensions
That is, it fixed the obligation on the provinces?
Yes.

Does the hon. gentleman
state that as his authority for saying that a bill passed by this House, assuming full responsibility, is ultra vires of this House?

It could be questioned. If
the action were voluntary it might possibly be so. But the point that was submitted was " Were these provinces right in saying that the sole responsibility rests on us?" The answer was, " The sole responsibility does not rest on you, but on the provinces." That was the point.

The hon. gentleman does
see from that opinion that the federal government might assume the responsibility, and the opinion of the Minister of Justice, expressed in a reply to a question of mine last year during the course of the debate, was in agreement with that.

The hon. member who has
just taken his seat made some reference to the unanimous way in which this legislation was received on that side of the House last year. Well, that is a matter of degree, I suppose. The Right Hon. Arthur Meigheu wanted to know what the cost of it would be, and those of us Who were there remember that he used this language; "I do not expect a close estimate at all, but say within a hundred million dollars or so." Then we find Sir Henry Drayton saying:
I am not at all certain that it is a good thing for this parliament to try and look after other business than its own. This is entirely a provincial matter.
Then we find the hon. member who represents West Calgary saying:
I do venture to plead with my hon. friends opposite to urge the government not to proceed with this at the present time.
Faint praise, surely. Then we find the hon. member for Muskoka asking:
Are we prepared at present to put everyone on the payroll of the country? It seems to me that we are getting into the habit in this parliament of going, I was going to say mad, in the way of such legislation.
That could hardly be called friendly comment and criticism. Then we find-I am speaking now from memory, but I know I can prove it if necessary-one gentleman referring to it as "impossible" legislation. Another one waxed more enthusiastic and said it was "a washout." Another member rose to the highest flights of his oratorical vocabulary and called it an "abortion." Poor comment, in

the light of the opinion of this gentleman who now claims that this legislation last year passed the House unanimously.
I recall that the bill was very much talked about in the last election, nowhere more so than in British Columbia. I recall a speech that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen made in opening the campaign, I think, in this city It was a great speech, worthy of a great man and a great occasion. I read it with much care, but I could find nothing in it on that subject which afterwards became so important in the campaign, that of old age pensions. You would have thought that a matter that was so much in the public mind, or at least was going to be, would have been foreshadowed in some way in this platform in which he was enunciating the program of his party in his appeal to the country. As a matter of fact I think I know when, and where, and how the hon. gentleman, like Paul at Damascus, got light on the subject. The right hon. gentleman came west. I am not familiar with the speeches he made along the line in his journey from the east to the west-hon. members from Saskatchewan and Alberta will be more familiar with that subject than I am; but I do know that I cannot recall any mention of old age pensions in his speeches, as a platform, until he reached British Columbia. I do not think there was any mention made of it even in Prince Rupert, the first place in the province where he spoke. He did me the honour to speak in the district of Comox-Albemi, and I have it on the authority of one of his own supporters, who told us of it at a public meeting, that he had said to Mr. Meighen, "Something has got to be done about old age pensions; people have asked about it and we know very little about it." Mr. Meighen said, "You shall have it." That is where the right hon. gentleman got his light and introduced the subject into his program. I have here, shown in big headlines, the announcement made by the Conservative organs the day after he made his next great speech in the city of Vancouver. The announcement in those headlines was, "Mr. Meighen declares himself at Vancouver meeting." Yes, he declared himself for the first time on that subject. Mr. Meighen dealt with old age pensions, the Australian treaty and co-operative marketing, but he put his contemplated promise of action on the subject of old age pensions first. Under the circumstances I think I am justified in saying that it was only when Mr. Meighen got into British Columbia and found out how urgent the situation was, how worked up public sentiment was, and how insistent the people of the province were.

Old Age Pensions
that he gave any explanation of his halfhearted support of, or to speak more truly, his attacks upon, old age pensions in the House. It was then he suddenly discovered that he was in favour of this legislation.
I will not at this stage of the resolution go into some of the comments that were made on this question during the last campaign and the attacks upon those of us who supported that legislation. Some of it was entirely comical in its attitude, and some of it was almost sad in the ignorance it displayed of those who were putting it forward, but I will deal with that perhaps on another occasion. I only hope this will not follow what happened last year. The country has certainly shown, as the hon. member for Wet-askiwin (Mr. Irvine) said, that no subject appeared to go so closely home to the hearts and minds and interests of the people during the last election campaign as this question of old age pensions, and it had more weight at the close than it had at the beginning of the campaign. I hope that the other honourable body of this parliament will realize when this bill comes up to them that they are not facing a party measure sent up by this House, whether as a party or by the whole House, but that they are facing the almost unanimous wish of the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, it is only
fitting that as the Labour member representing East Calgary I should put my views on record regarding this measure. I fully agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I would prefer a purely federal measure, and there are many amendments I would like to see made when the bill comes down. I would prefer the age limit to be sixty-five instead of seventy years. But I regard this as a stepping stone to better things. We have in the measure before us a fifty-fifty proposition. I had hoped that the government would make it a sixty-forty proposition, and perhaps if this measure should prove a success they will yet make it a sixty-forty proposition, and perhaps by-and-by a seventy-five-twenty-five proposition, and ultimately perhaps a purely federal measure.
There is one thing quite sure, that this measure was discussed on nearly all the platforms in the last campaign, and there was no measure presented to the people in my *constituency at all events which contributed more to the success of myself and the Liberal candidates generally than this one, and it was entirely on a fifty-fifty basis. As to the characterization of this measure by my hon. friends who opposed me in that election,
I remember particularly the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen himself when he visited the Pavilion at Calgary describing the proposed legislation in these words: " It is a sham; it is a Sham; it is a sham." These words echoed and re-echoed throughout my constituency in connection with this fifty-fifty proposition, but I am glad to see my friends to my right perfectly willing now to support a measure which erstwhile they called "a sham, a sham, a sham." Not only did they call it that, but they advocated a measure that would be entirely contributory, and which if it had passed would have entirely left out those who could not contribute, whereas this measure is put forward, I believe, for the benefit of those who are unable to contribute in their old age.
If the provinces should not fall in line with this measure, the only thing that can be said is that they are not obeying the dictates of the people: they are not considering what was in the hearts and in the minds of the people in the election campaign of last September, and in that campaign the old age pension scheme contributed more largely to the success of the Liberal candidates than any other measure put before the people.
There is another matter which I think deserves attention. It has been stated here tonight that this measure would be imposing something on the provinces against their will. The other side :of the question is more correct.: It will be relieving the provinces of fifty per cent of their obligations in 'maintaining their poor. I have been associated with the relief department of the city of Calgary, and the gentleman who is now the manager of that department told me that he was looking forward to the time when even this fifty-fifty measure would become law, for he said that the number of old people in that city who required assistance and had to be kept by the city was growing every year, and that if this measure should pass it would relieve the city of many thousands of dollars it would otherwise have to pay out in relieving these old people.
I do not think I need say anything more at this stage. While I would have preferred a purely federal measure, and while I submit for the consideration of the Minister of Labour that he put this measure on a sixty-forty basis instead of a fifty-fifty, and while I hope that he will make the minimum age 65 instead of 70 years, if he cannot see his way to making these 'changes I shall 'have bo support the measure as it is.
Old Age Pensions

At this stage I shall occupy the time of the icommitfee very briefly indeed, because my leader has fairly and fully set before the House his attitude, which corresponds I think with the attitude of hon. members who sit behind him. I know that he has expressed very fully and very clearly my views upon this question.
This is a very important measure, and it is much in the minds ard seriously occupying the attention of the people of Canada at this time. Unfortunately the matter was one of considerable controversy in the last election, and I can only say that the attitude of those who sit on this side of the House was much misrepresented indeed in the last campaign. Speaking for myself, I was pictured first as one who had voted against this measure, although there was no vote upon it: it carried without a vote. Then when that was pointed out to be incorrect, it was asserted that I opposed the measure, but Hansard will be searched in vain for one sentenJce uttered by me in opposition to this measure. I am in favour now, as I was in favour then, of old age pensions, but I believe that whatever is worth doing is worth doing well, and I suggest that this measure is not doing justice to the question. If we are to have a wholehearted scheme of old age pensions, then this parliament should deal with it exclusively and should not make libs grant conditional upon a grant by the provinces. I am afraid that a great many of the old people who are expecting old age pensions will be keenly disappointed, because, unless the provinces adopt the scheme there will be no pension for them. As one speaker has said, it will be a case of Old Mother Hubbard going to the cupboard, and when she gets there finding it bare. That is about all I have to say at this stage of the debate. When the bill is in committee I may have some further observations to make.
In conclusion, I want to say that there is an element of unfairness and injustice in this bill, because a province that does not adopt a system of old age pensions will be called upon indirectly to pay its proportion of the cost of old age pensions in every other province that does adopt the system. That is a serious matter to Ontario, to Quebec, and to all the other provinces, but notwithstanding that injustice, notwithstanding that defect, and because it is, if nothing else, at least a gesture in the direction of old age pensions, I am going to support this measure. I would much more heartily support a measure that would ensure at once bring about for the deserving old people of Canada an immediate

pension. I fear this only puts it off, but if we oppose it we shall be charged with placing obstacles in the way of this measure. For that reason, while not satisfied with it as a wholehearted, substantial measure, I am going to give it my support.

Might I suggest to my right hon. friend that it might be a good thing if the committee were to rise now and we take up another order of business? There are still many on this side who desire to speak on this question.

speechtext: If there is a desire to have this discussion prolonged, I agree that the suggestion made by my hon. friend is much to the point. I was hoping that we might pass the resolution to-night. If it is the wish of hon. gentlemen opposite to continue there will be an opportunity on the bill for any who may wish to speak. We might perhaps agree on passing the resolution, and then have a further discussion on the bill.

I have an idea that if we have the discussion on the resolution, the bill will pass much more speedily than if we allow the discussion to go over on the bill. I know there are still several on this side who desire to speak on the question, and as I understand there is other 'business to be done to-night, it might be well to let the committee rise now.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
On the Votes and Proceedings of to-day, hon. members will see a notice that I have given of a resolution which reads:
That from and out of the consolidated revenue fund there may be paid and applied a sum not exceeding $250,000 towards defraying any expenses that may be incurred for the celebration of the sixtieth anniversary of confederation.
I understand that the Senate in all probability will conclude its sittings this week, and will then adjourn for some little time. It is

Diamond Jubilee of Confederation
desirable, that as rapid progress as possible should be made with the formation of the committee to have charge of the celebration of the diamond jubilee of confederation, and if the House will grant its unanimous consent, I should like to have permission to introduce this resolution to-night and if possible to introduce as well the bill which in this connection, the government proposes to introduce. I might say that I have before me an important precedent for this procedure. AVhen the House was asked to give its approval to the treaty of Peace between the allied and associated powers and Germany, Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister, on the afternoon of the 4th September, 1919, asked the House to agree to a resolution, notice of which had just been given in the Votes and Proceedings. I would like to ask the House now to allow me to 'have this resolution placed on the order paper for consideration as for this date, and if it is passed I will introduce the bill based upon it. I beg to move:
That it be resolved that the proposed resolution as it appears as a notice of motion in the Votes and Proceedings of the 14th instant, as follows:
"Resolved, that from and out of the consolidated revenue fund there may be paid and applied a sum not exceeding $250,000 towards defraying any expenses that may be incurred for tlie celebration of the sixtieth anniversary of confederation"
be placed on the order paper for consideration this day.

Motion agreed to.

I shall be very happy to give my hon. friend the information as soon as His Honour the Speaker leaves the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It has been
thought by the government that the management of the celebration would be better effected if the whole matter, rather than being dealt with departmentally, were put into the hands of a national committee, this national. committee to form an executive committee; the executive committee to be given the powers that will be set forth in the bill which will be introduced. I might say that the government is following in this regard the example that was set by a previous administration with respect to the administration of the Canadian patriotic fund. When the committee for the administration of the Canadian patriotic fund was formed, a number of gentlemen were named, because of their representative positions, as members of a provisional committee. The provisional committee was fairly large. It held one meeting at which it selected certain of its numbers and others who were not of its membership as members of an executive committee. This committee held meetings at regular intervals during the time that the fund was in existence. .
It is proposed in the bill that will be introduced to incorporate a body to be known as the national committee for the celebration of the diamond jubilee of confederation. The personnel will consist of Their Excellencies the Governor General and the Viscountess Willingdon, the lieutenant governors of the several provinces, the premiers of the several provinces, the Speakers of the House of Commons and the Senate, a few members of His Majesty's Privy Council for Canada, a few senators, the Chief Justice of Canada, the deputy heads of certain of the departments of the public service, the presidents of the two large railway systems, the heads of a few representative organizations of Canada, among the number being the President of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League, the President of the Canadian Battlefields Memorial Association, the President of the National Council of Women of Canada, the President of the Imperial Order of Daughters of the Empire, the President of the Daughters of Canada, the one lady member of this House of Commons, the chairman of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, the chairman of the Executive Committee of the Association of Canadian Clubs. I think I have summarized those whose names are mentioned as being among those of the committee to be incorporated and regarded as the provisional committee. The names have been chosen regardless of party affiliation and with the view as far as
350	COMMONS
Diamond Jubilee of Confederation
possible of making the committee representative of the whole of the Dominion. Naturally there are many organizations that might appropriately find a place in its membership, but if a beginning is made in one direction it will have to be followed in Others and this will involve the addition of a very large number of names. I should like the House to understand that this is a provisional committee, and that it will have power to add any names that in its wisdom it may deem desirable.
The bill gives the committee .power to receive moneys the parliament may appropriate or any moneys that may .be contributed for the purpose, and allows it to determine how the money is to be spent. In other words, the government is not desirous of dictating the particular programme which shall be adopted by the Dominion with respect to a great national celebration of this kind. We think it will meet with .more general satisfaction on the part of the public if a representative body such as this is given power to make all the arrangements that may be necessary.
I may say to my iron, friend that communications have come from a very large number of sources containing all kinds of suggestions, from pageants to the publication of histories, and other schemes too numerous to mention. The government proposes to turn over to this committee all the suggestions that it may receive and to place upon the committee the responsibility of deciding what shall be done.
May I say to hon. members, so that they will have reason to know there is no effort to prevent the fullest discussion as to how this money shall be spent, that the House will be given an opportunity bo discuss the matter when the estimates are under consideration, because this item of $250,000 will have to be voted in supply. The committee will have to have -its accounts audited and will have to make to parliament a full statement of how it has conducted its affairs.

It depends
entirely upon what the -committee recommends. The committee may come to parliament with a request for an additional vote, but so far as public funds are concerned, I would say, that the committee will be restricted to the amounts given to it by parliament. One of the
purposes of having this committee formed is that it may immediately get in touch with the provinces and if possible work out some form of joint celebration. A number of municipalities will no doubt also wish to have their own celebrations. This committee will seek to coordinate efforts from one end of .the Dominion to the other, as they relate to provinces or to municipalities, with whatever the federal government may attempt.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I point out -that in the -outline the Prime Minister has given us, although he says that the appointment of this committee -will be entirely irrespective of party, its personnel is very largely political in character? The organizations mentioned are of a particular type, they are not in any sense .representative of all the different classes of the people of Canada. As I 'think of the people -who have made confederation worth while, I think of the large farming population in every one of these provinces, yet so far as the Prime Minister has intimated -there is no farmer appointed on any of these committees. We have large farm organizations in each of the three prairie provinces which I kno-w best-very large and very representative farm organizations, both men's and women's-and yet apparently these have been entirely overlooked. I think of the particular group which I have been representing in .this House, the labour group in each of the provinces. I suppose there are over 150 distinct labour organizations in Canada representing the rank and file of the people who are contributing very largely to the upbuilding of this country. Apparently they are entirely overlooked in the outline which has been given us by the Prime Minister. If a celebration of this kind is to be made of any very great educational value, I should think that those who would be in the very forefront would be the representatives of our educational system, members of the universities, -and especially school' teachers. We have school teachers' organizations in almost every province of the Dominion to-day. These school teachers are in touch with a very large proportion of our population, that is, the younger part that is attending school, the most impressionable part, and they ought to be most interested in a celebration of this kind. These teachers are apparently overlooked in the selection that has been made of the people who are to determine what character

Select Standing Committees
will be given to this event. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that these matters require a little further consideration than would appear to have been given them from the outline that has been so far presented to us.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I say to my hon. friend that I think he would be nearer the mark if he were to recognize that persons holding representative positions, such as the lieutenant governors of the several provinces hold, such as the premiers hold, such as the hon. Speaker of this House holds, represent in a broad way, all classes. They are not chosen from any one particular class, they are chosen because they happen, to fill representative positions that are broad enough to include all groups. My hon. friend says that no recognition has been given to the agricultural class. As I understand it, the Premier of Manitoba is a graduate of an agricultural college and a well-known agriculturist, and I am sure that so far as agriculture might need special representation he is splendidly fitted to give it. The Premier of Alberta, although a lawyer, is the head of a government which is recognized as a farmers government.

speechtext:
Yes, and the
Premier of Saskatchewan. I did draw particular attention to the fact that the government had placed among these names, the name of the hon. member for Southeast Grey. I think if anyone in this House has given attention to agricultural problems the hon. member for Southeast Grey is entitled to special recognition in that regard. As I have already said, the committee is a provisional committee. Undoubtedly when it comes to determining the executive there will be included many persons whose names would come within special groups. As a matter of fact, in considering the subject, a number of names were suggested, for example, the name o.f Mr. Tom Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Council, was proposed. It was pointed out that if Mr. Moore was to be on the committee then representation ought to be given also to the manufacturers' association, and if the manufacturers' association then the chambers of commerce; then some other organizations would be entitled to representation. And so it would run on; any number of organizations might be included. If it were the intention to embrace every organization that may wish to take part in this celebration, I am afraid we would have a committee incapable of functioning.
This much said, may I add that I think my hon. friend has been quite right in directing the attention of the committee to the importance of seeing that all classes are represented, and I shall be very much astonished if, when this provisional committee meets, any class that desires to have special recognition in connection with the program is not given every opportunity of having its voice heard and its interests considered.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: With respect to the committee that has been mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I still feel that an omission of great importance is noticed. I do feel that the diamond jubilee of confederation is of such far-reaching importance that the educational aspect of it should be given great prominence. It will be a wonderful time among the youth of Canada and I consider that the chancellor or the president or the representative direct of the educational system of Canada should receive recognition. I know myself what it will mean if we enable the youth of Canada to come to a realization of the past history, of the Dominion, and to form some idea of its unity in the future. I therefore respectfully request that the university system of Canada, as represented either by a chancellor or by a president, receive special mention in that particular committee which has been referred to this evening.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will run through the list of names he will find that a large percentage are those of university graduates, and he may, I think, rest absolutely assured that in the hands of that provisional committee, the educational interests of the country will be well taken care of when the executive committee comes to be formed.
